paragraphs.text: Würzburg Codex Mp. th. q. 3, written in the fifth or sixth century.

With the sign I I have marked the end of a page; with II, the end of a leaf; with ', the end of a line (in the critical apparatus); and with i [?] I have enclosed what survives in an erasure where it cannot be said what was written there before.

Our faith is hindered by no stumbling-blocks in our life, and it holds to the secure path of catholic order toward God, so it is free. Yet when it is attacked by the devil's slander, it is proved all the more in the very place where it is struck. So, most blessed bishops, we have thought it a glorious thing for us to speak. Our conscience does not accuse us. In frequent tracts we have set out our faith and condemned the doctrines of all heretics. In the tract of our brothers Tiberianus, Asarbus and the rest, with whom we share one faith and one mind, every doctrine that seems to be against Christ has been condemned, and every doctrine that is for Christ approved. Nevertheless, even now, because you wish it, and because, as it is written, we are always ready to make confession to everyone who asks us for a reason for the faith and hope that is in us, we have not been willing to keep silent about what you command. All our life is open before your eyes, and since we stand in the light of faith we pursue no hidden secrets of a dark way of life. Even so, we have not refused to repeat our confession, so that satisfaction might be given even to those who do not know us, and so that no one, believing ill of us, might sin through another's [?] error. We have not refused to show with our mouths what we believed in our hearts.

We ought not to boast of what we once were. Still, we were not born into the world in so obscure a place, nor were we called so foolish, that the faith of Christ and instruction in belief could have brought us death rather than salvation. As you yourselves know, we came to this faith after we had gone through every experience of human life and rejected our evil ways, and we entered it as a harbour of secure rest. We recognized that no one would ascend into the kingdom of heaven unless he was reborn of water and the Holy Spirit. So through the Spirit we purified our souls to obey the faith. We rejected the desires of our former life, of which we were ashamed, and for the path of renewed grace we received the creed of catholic observance, which we still hold. We did this so that we might enter the washing, which is the redemption of our body, and be baptized in Christ and put on Christ, and so that, spurning the empty glory of the world, we might give our life to him alone, as we had already given it. He granted us the forgiveness of sins, himself suffered for us, and gave our souls both redemption and salvation. For who is there who reads the Scriptures and believes in one faith, one

baptism and one God, and does not condemn the foolish doctrines of the heretics? Because they wish to compare divine things with human ones, they divide the substance that is united in the power of God. By the crime of the Binionites [?] they split up the greatness of Christ, which is venerated in the threefold font of the church. Yet it is written: “I am God, and there is no other besides me; there is no righteous one and saviour besides me.” And: “I am the first, and I am hereafter, and besides me there is no God; who is like me?” And elsewhere: “I am, and before me there was no other, and after me there will be none like me; I am God, and there is none besides me who saves.” And again Moses says: “The Lord our God is one God.” And Jeremiah says: “This is our God, and no other shall be reckoned beside him, who found the whole way of wisdom and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved; afterwards he was seen on earth and lived among men.” For he is the one who was, who is and who is to come. He was seen from the ages. As the Word made flesh he dwelt in us. He was crucified, overcame death, and became heir of life. He rose on the third day and became the pattern of what is to come, showing the hope of our resurrection. And ascending

into heaven, he builds a road for those who come to him. He is wholly in the Father and the Father is in him, so that what is written might be made clear: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.” As John says: “There are three that bear witness on earth: the water, the flesh and the blood, and these three are in one. And there are three that bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word and the Spirit, and these three are one in Christ Jesus.”

You wish us to go through each point and declare what we believe. It is rather our place to be eager to learn from you. Yet God, though he showed by his works who he was, still wished to hear from his disciples who he was and who he was believed to be. In keeping with God's example, then, and because you also wish us to prove to you what you already know, we ask your pardon if we speak at some length, either in asserting our faith or in demolishing what error insinuates in order to corrupt the minds of unbelievers. The fault belongs to those who tell many lies against Christ's people and so have made us reject at greater length the charges they bring [?]. Let him be anathema who believes the evil of the Patripassian heresy and the catholic faith

…is troubling, since it is written, in Peter's words: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God"; and elsewhere: "Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son does not have life"; and again, in his own words: "I and the Father are one"; and elsewhere: "I am in the Father and the Father is in me." To bear witness to this there is also the confession of the demons in the Gospel, saying: "You are the Christ, the Son of God; why have you come before the time to destroy us?" We know that this was set down not because God wanted the testimony of demons, but so that human beings, made in the image and likeness of God, would be bound over to worse torments if they did not know what even the demons confess. For us, however, there is one God the Father, from whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him. To their folly is added the Novatian heresy, as though, while the error of sin keeps growing worse, people could be cleansed by repeated baptisms. Yet apostolic scripture testifies to one baptism, one faith, one God, and we know that beyond what has been preached to us, not even an angel from heaven is to be heard if he says otherwise. But we, baptized once in Christ, leave behind what is past and stretch forward to what lies ahead,

and wish to lay hold of that for which we have been laid hold of. For apart from the one Christ Jesus, united in faith, we have no protection other than that of the one baptism, knowing that Christ came in the flesh to save sinners, and, having redeemed them in himself, to restore them to the ordinances of eternal life. But whoever denies that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is the antichrist, and his destruction will not slumber, as the apostle says: "Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father either; but whoever confesses the Son has both the Son and the Father." Anathema be the doctrine of the Nicolaitans, and let anyone who either institutes or follows sacrileges hateful to God have his portion with Sodom and Gomorrah. Anathema be anyone who reads of griffins, eagles, asses, elephants, serpents and useless beasts, and, held captive by the vanity of a confused observance, sets them up as a mystery of divine religion, when their works and their detestable forms belong to the nature of demons, not to the truth of divine glories. For these are the ones whose god is the belly and whose glory is in their shame; these are the ones who overturn the wavering

and lead them to the ruin of their own perdition, and call it a sacrament, not knowing that according to the scriptures of God it is a mystery of perdition. Going headlong over the precipice, as the prophet says, they have become like wind in the wings of birds, and so they will be put to shame by their shrines, having become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding; and they deserve to have the Sun for their god. But we, taught by the words of the divine scriptures, although we know that an idol is nothing in this world, and that what they sacrifice they sacrifice to demons and not to God, nevertheless strive, as it is written, to understand the subtleties of words and the interpretations of parables, and to act as those who are in God, so that nothing in us may bear the shape of beasts, but the discipline of Christ God may hold the whole of us. For there is no fellowship between the table of the Lord and the table of demons, between light and darkness, between Christ and Belial. As John also says, speaking of such things: "If anyone worships the beast and its image, he has received a mark on his forehead and on his hand"; and he says elsewhere: "I saw a beast rising from the sea, having ten horns

and seven heads, and on its heads ten diadems and a blasphemous name; and it was like a leopard, its feet were like a bear's and its mouth like a lion's mouth, and the dragon gave it his throne and his power." Daniel too says of this very thing: "I was watching, and behold, the four winds were stirring up the great sea, and four beasts were coming up out of the sea, each surpassing the other in size. The first was like a lioness, and its wings were like an eagle's; and it was lifted from the ground and stood on a man's feet, and a man's heart was given to it. And behold, another beast, like a bear, and it stood on one side, and three ribs were in its mouth between its teeth; and it was told: 'Arise, devour the flesh of many.' And behold, another beast like a leopard, and it had four wings of a bird, and the beast had four heads, and power was given to it. And behold, a fourth beast, terrible and astonishing and exceedingly strong, and its teeth were of iron and its claws of bronze." All these things, set down in their visions, the prophets wished to be read by all and, once understood, to be shunned. And so those who knew these things but did not rightly understand what it was they were reading have had their heart given to the beast,

and their flesh will be devoured. For they became futile in their thinking and their foolish heart was darkened; claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man and of birds and four-footed animals and serpents; and, conforming themselves to the former desires of their life of ignorance, they have fallen into things they do not understand. But we know that the law is spiritual and that all prophecy needs interpretation, and we have Christ God in our understanding to show us the way; through him, even when we thought otherwise, these things too were revealed to us. So we have resolved to serve the righteousness of the Lord unto sanctification, so that, as the prophet says, having rooted the names of the Baals out of our mouth and blotted out their titles, we may cast away from us, as it is written, the covenant that is made with the beasts of the field and the birds of the sky and the creeping things of the earth, recognizing that all these are the wages of sin, whose end is death, whereas grace and peace are eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. As Solomon too says:

"God has given me true knowledge of all things that are: to know the order of the world and the power of the elements, the beginning and end and middle of the months, the changes and divisions of the seasons, the course of the year and the positions of the stars, the natures of animals and the rage of wild beasts, the force of the winds and the thoughts of men, the varieties of trees and the powers of roots; and I have come to know all things, both hidden and manifest." As he also says: "Some in their error worshiped mute reptiles and serpents and useless beasts, and he sent upon them a multitude of mute animals in vengeance, so that they might know that a man is punished by the very things through which he sins." As David too says: "Many calves surrounded me, fat bulls besieged me; they opened their mouths against me like a lion ravening and roaring." Let the impure mind of the schismatics take note as it reads this, and if it can be converted and can escape perishing, let it not perish. For holy David did not fear bulls or calves, but, as it is written:

"Your adversary the devil, like a ravening and roaring lion, prowls around seeking someone to devour; resist him, firm in the faith." As it is also written elsewhere: "Do not be a lion in your house, overturning your household"; and as it says there too: "Do not exalt yourself in the thoughts of your soul like a bull, lest your strength be dashed down and through folly it eat up your leaves." As David too says: "My tongue has stuck to my jaws, and you have brought me down into the dust of death, for many dogs have surrounded me"; yet here holy David, to show what he had meant by that earlier cry, added: "The assembly of sinners has besieged me." As Isaiah too says: "The dogs are souls that never know satiety." So too the Lord our God, speaking to the prophet Job, said: "Show me whether the lion now submits to you, or whether the unicorn will serve you or sleep in its stall"; and elsewhere God says to him: "You will capture Leosibora [?]; you will fill the souls of dragons with fear, so that they are afraid as they sit in their lairs in the woods and plot deceit"; and again elsewhere the Lord says to him:

"Will you draw out the dragon with a hook, or put a halter in its nose, or pierce its lips, and will it speak softly to you and make a covenant with you, so that you have it as your slave forever?" Here holy Job, understanding that the Lord was speaking, and wishing to open the understanding of these words to us as well, says: "Why am I still being judged, Lord, as I am rebuked and reproved? Or what answer shall I give, Lord, to such words, since I am nothing?" And then the Lord, granting to us also who were to come afterward the work of the word so that we might understand him, explained the parable of the discourse spoken through him, saying: "Do not set aside my judgment, and do not suppose that I have decreed anything other than that you might appear less unrighteous. But take up loftiness and power, and clothe yourself with glory and honor; leave the angels of wrath behind, and extinguish everything injurious and proud in you; break the wicked away from you and hide them in the earth, and fill their faces with disgrace, so that they may be without honor; and then you will confess that my right hand is able to save you. Even before you the wild beast, become like an ox, eats hay; its strength is in its loins and its power in the navel of its belly, and its tail is erect like a cypress,

its sinews are twisted like ropes, its sides are rocks of bronze, and its spine is like an iron wall; and this is the beginning, made for the angels to mock my creation." Yet searching the scriptures in all these things, most blessed priests, we know that they were written for our sake, so that whoever understands the natures of the beasts spoken of in parables may reject the ways of the world and chastise the vices within himself. As it is written in the Apocalypse: "Behold, the waters you saw, where the harlot sits, are peoples and multitudes and nations and tongues." As John also says there: "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, and she has become a dwelling place of demons, because the nations have drunk of the wrath of her fornication"; and he says there too: "And they will weep and beat their breasts over her, because they committed fornication with her and lived in her luxury." As the apostle too says: "Your struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the princes and powers of this world, the rulers of this darkness, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places." As John too says: "I saw coming out of the mouth of the dragon and out of the mouth of the beast and out of the mouth of the false prophet three

unclean spirits like frogs; and these are spirits of demons, which perform signs and go forth to throw the kings of the earth into confusion." In short, as those initiated in Christ, we hold fast to the first rudiments of the faith we received. We know that what we believed, we believed in God, and what we renounced, we renounced in the devil; that he is the one called the beast, and that God is the one who is Christ Jesus. As the apostle too says: "For it is not for oxen that God is concerned, but he speaks of us, since the one who plows ought to plow in hope, and the one who threshes ought to receive the fruit of his hope." So let no one ascribe to us an understanding that springs from his own perversity; each will be condemned by his own words and justified by his own words. We confess what we believe, and, searching the scriptures and rejecting the appearance of demons, we understand, as it is written, the depths of Satan, knowing, as the apostle says, that no one has freed us from the body of this death except the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ. For it is written: "Unless you believe, you will not understand"; and elsewhere: "Good understanding to all who practice it."

As for the fact, most blessed priests, that they have brought forward idolatrous figures, Saturn, Venus, Mercury, Jupiter, Mars and the other gods of the gentiles: even if we were living quite idle toward God, with no faith instructed by the scriptures, still, back when we took delight in the ways of worldly folly, we recognized through secular learning, useless to us though it was, that these things were opposed to our faith; and seeing through the gods of the gentiles, we laughed at the worldly follies and misfortunes of those whose works we used to read as a kind of training for the mind. But if the faith of our profession is being examined even on these matters, then anathema be he—and let their table become a snare and a stumbling block to them—who calls gods the Sun and Moon, Jupiter, Mars, Mercury, Venus or Saturn and all the host of heaven, which the error of the gentiles, ignorant of God, has adopted for itself in the ceremonies of its sacred rites, and who venerates them, though they are detestable idols worthy of hell. For it is written: "Woe to him who says to wood, 'Wake up and rise,' and to stone, 'Be exalted.'" Let them perish with their gods, whether these are said to be in heaven or on earth; let the boar from the forest, as it is written, ravage the vine of their understanding,

and the solitary wild beast feed on it. But for us, who have been set free from the body of this death through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, as it is written, "a thousand will fall at your side and ten thousand at your right hand," so that, clothed according to the scriptures in the armor of God, we may tread upon the basilisk and the asp and trample the lion and the dragon, subject to no likeness of the misery of idols. Of this it is written: "What profit is the carved image, because it has been carved? They fashioned it as a molten thing, a false phantom, and those who formed it are put to shame over their own figment, for the idols were deaf." The reason why the foolish superstitions of idols, or the forms of sins, or the names of demons, or the death that vices bring are shown to us is this: that, understanding the darkness, we may long for the light of the Lord, and, crying out, "Know, you nations, that God is with us," may burst their bonds and cast their yoke from us, and not be defiled, as it is written, by the practices of the Egyptians, since the Lord will laugh at them and the Lord will deride them. Of these John, pointing out the prince of the misery of idols, says: "He is one of the seven, and is the eighth, and goes to perdition";

and of these Solomon too says: "Do not sow in the furrows of iniquity, and you will not reap them sevenfold"; for so he says elsewhere as well: "Before man are life and death, water and fire; let him stretch out his hand to whichever he wishes." For these are the seven shepherds and the eight bites [?] of men, working, as it is written, in the sons of unbelief. But for us to live is Christ; Christ is life, Christ is faith. We know that we have an anointing from the Holy One, and that we were redeemed from the empty way of life handed down by our fathers not with perishable silver and gold, but with the precious blood, as of a lamb undefiled and spotless, Jesus Christ; and since we are established in him, let no one despoil us through the philosophy of the world rather than according to Christ. Let those who love gold invent for themselves a golden age of Saturn; for us divine wisdom is more precious than all gold and silver and precious stone. Let those whose dwelling is the fire of hell call the Sun their god, and let those who do not want Christ God as their beginning confess that they belong to his element; for us all things under the sun are vanity and the presumption of a perverse spirit, and we know that he will perish with the world. Let those in their wickedness confess the Moon as a god who, carried about by every wind of doctrine,

set themselves to observe days and seasons and years and months. Let those call Mars their god who have taken their pleasure in Mars the adulterer and, given over to the lust of the flesh, are bound by fornications; and, having become like sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal, let them reckon Jupiter their god, destined to perish with him, their father and author. But for us God is Christ Jesus, who, when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with him, forgiving us all our trespasses and blotting out the handwriting that stood against us, which was hostile to us with its decrees; and he took it out of the way, nailing it to the cross. He boldly led the principalities and powers away, triumphing over them in himself. For those who worship such demons will be struck down like their gods by the sword of the Lord, and, not knowing the true Father and Christ God, the Son of God, they will be seen to have become like their idols, as it is written: "Father against son, son against father, daughter-in-law against mother-in-law, mother-in-law against daughter-in-law, and a man's enemies will be those of his own household." Let those worship Mercury as a god who acquire moth-eaten purses of earthly treasure and venerate his caduceus or his purse; we seek treasures hidden in heaven and

unseen, which rust does not seize nor moth corrupt, knowing that the rich man has not entered the kingdom of heaven, as it is written: "Come now, you rich, weep and howl over the miseries that are coming upon your riches. Your garments have rotted and are moth-eaten; your gold and your silver, which you have stored up, will rust in the last days, and their rust will be a testimony against you and will eat your flesh like fire." But we know that God has chosen the poor of the world, rich in faith, to be heirs of the kingdom. Let those venerate Venus as a god who commit shameful acts and await the fitting recompense of their error. But we look to Abraham our father and to Sarah who bore us; born of mother Church and brought forth with Wisdom as our midwife, we press on toward the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ, until we all attain to the unity of the faith and the knowledge of the Son of God, to the perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ. And although no one is sufficient for these things,

we nevertheless know that our God is mighty, since he who promised is able also to perform it; for he himself said: "Who has hoped in the Lord and been put to shame, or has remained in his commandments and been forsaken?"

Anathema be anyone who venerates Sacla, Nebroel, Samael, Beelzebub, Nasbodeus, Belial and all such—for they are demons—with the wretched hallowing of ceremonies, or says that they ought to be venerated. All of these, as we read in the scriptures of God, we condemn, scorning the claims of demonic wisdom. For into whatever appearances and forms the devil may [?] change himself, we know that he can be nothing other than the devil. Whether he is called Abaddon in Hebrew, or Apollyon in Greek, or Exterminans, "the Destroyer," in Latin, or whether he is presented as a beast with seven heads and ten horns, or as a serpent or a dragon, we know that he is the devil, after the manner of the prince of the power of this air, the spirit that works in the sons of unbelief, among whom we too all once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the will of the flesh and of our thoughts. Of him it is written in the Apocalypse: "And the great dragon was cast down from heaven, the ancient serpent who is called the devil and Satan, who led the whole world astray; he was cast down to the earth, and his angels were cast down with him."

And so it is no wonder if those who believe in such beings, or sanctify themselves under such an author, being by nature children of wrath and perdition and walking in darkness, deny in themselves the image and likeness of God, become like the devil in their vices, and ascribe the making of man to demons. Of them the apostle rightly says: "The natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God; nor can he, for they are folly to him and he cannot judge them. But the spiritual man judges all things, yet he himself is judged by no one." And as it is written: "Those who are of the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who are of the spirit on the things of the spirit; and the wisdom of the flesh is death, but the wisdom of the spirit is life and peace."

And if they wish to know what we think about each of the things that are written: such people rightly share kinship with the earthly Adam, who became a beast of a darkened life, as it is written: "As was the earthly one, so too are those who are earthly; as is the heavenly one, so too are those who are heavenly." They deserve to be among those whom Eve brought forth in the form of Cain and Lamech, she who had been made

…the mother of all the living, who committed adultery against God and gave in to the devil's seduction, called the demon Saclas both her god and her husband. As it is written in the prophet: "Behold, bring judgment against your mother, for she is not my wife, nor am I her husband; and I will take away her fornication from the face of my people, and her adultery from between her breasts." And again in the same place: "And I will take away my garments and my linen, so that she may not cover her shame, and I will lay bare her filthiness in the sight of her lovers." And in Jeremiah the Lord rebukes Jerusalem, which had been made a slave along with her children, and says to her: "How can you say, 'I am not defiled, and I have not gone after Baal'? Look at your many ways, and see where you have not committed fornication." And Ezekiel says: "Thus says the Lord: 'Your root is from the land of Canaan; your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite.'" Likewise elsewhere: "I have likened your mother to the night; my people is like one who has no knowledge." So too in the gospel God says to such people: "You are children of the devil, and you have the devil as your father." But that is not how we learned Christ. Rather, having been taught in

him, as the truth is in Jesus, we understand that the law is spiritual, but we are carnal, sold under sin. Comparing spiritual things with spiritual, we strive that, just as we bore the image of him who is of clay when, overcome by our offenses, we walked in vices, so we may bear the image of him who is from heaven. Putting off the old man of our former way of life, who is corrupted by the desires of error, we strive to be renewed in the spirit of our mind and to put on the new man, who has been created according to God in holiness, righteousness and truth. For we know and recognize that we are God's handiwork for good works, which God prepared so that we should walk in them. As Moses also says: "God made man in his image and likeness, and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul." And we know that Eve, who was deceived and fell into transgression, will be saved through bearing children, if she continues in faith and acknowledges that she was taken from her husband; and bearing children in sorrow, she will turn back to her husband,

as it is written in the prophet: "Therefore, behold, says the Lord, I will hedge up your mother's way with stakes, and I will not build her road, and she will not find her paths. She will pursue her lovers and will not overtake them, and she will say, 'I will go and return to my former husband, for it was better for me then than now.'" Understanding this, we have been set free, as it is written, from our mother's womb. Not yielding to flesh and blood, we strive, and as we were once slaves of sin unto death, so now we are slaves of righteousness unto righteousness. We know that even if our outer man is being corrupted, the inner man is being renewed. And as the first man was from the earth, of clay, so the works of the flesh are plain: adulteries, fornication, impurity, licentiousness, lust, idolatry, sorceries, enmities, strife, jealousies, fits of anger, quarrels, dissensions, heresies, envyings, murders, drunkenness, carousing, and things like these. Among these let the demons Saclas and Nebroel have their share among their own kind; let them not look for a place among things chaste and religious.

And as the second man is from heaven, heavenly, so the works of the spirit are plain: love, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, gentleness, faith, self-control, chastity, kindness and affection. In this Christ, appearing as God, said that we are his temple, and he willed to dwell in us, in what he himself had made for himself in us. As the prophet Job also says: "Your hands formed me and made me; afterward you changed and cast me down. Remember that you fashioned me of clay from the earth and called me back again. You milked me like milk and curdled me like cheese; you clothed me with skin and flesh, you knit together bones and sinews; you set life and mercy within me, and your care has guarded my spirit."

And therefore we repeat the word again and again: Anathema be anyone who denies that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, for this is the antichrist. Anathema be anyone who denies that Christ Jesus, God, the Son of God, was crucified for us, since the prophet says, "He bears our sins and suffers for us," and Paul again testifies that he knows nothing but Jesus Christ and him crucified. Anathema be anyone who denies that our Lord God was fastened with nails or given vinegar or gall to drink, since he himself said to his disciples:

"Put your hands into the clefts of the wounds of my hands"; and we read in the gospel: "And they took a sponge full of vinegar and gall and gave him to drink, and he said, 'It is finished.'" Schismatics or heretics have tampered with all these scriptures to suit their own scheme, inserting the sense of their own wretchedness into the divine words, and so have mixed falsehood with truth and lies with catholic teaching.

Anathema be anyone who does not condemn Mani and his works, doctrines and practices. If it were possible, we would pursue their shameful practices in particular with the sword and send them down to the underworld, or to anything worse than Gehenna and its unsleeping torment, where the fire is not quenched and the worm does not die. And so that their impurity might not escape the divine judgment, their evils have been exposed even in the secular courts. For besides holding, in their wandering minds, that the Sun and the Moon are gods and rulers of the world, although it is written, "What is brighter than the sun? Yet even it will fail," they have carried the folly of their wretched sacrileges so far as to claim that the more wickedly they bound minds overwhelmed by blindness, the more religiously they consecrated them. Anathema be anyone who does not condemn the fornications of the Nicolaitans and the manifold

demons shown in the scriptures, together with their disciples and teachers, or anyone who follows their works. Let those perish who have taken the perfidy of the Ophites into themselves and, having become a brood of vipers, confess a god and lord like themselves. And since it would take too long to go through them one by one, we condemn all the heresies that men corrupt in mind and shipwrecked in faith have fabricated for themselves, whether from the canonical scriptures or from apocrypha, going beyond what is written, each puffed up against another on behalf of someone else: whatever the Saturninian heresy introduced, or the Novatian brought forth, or Basilides displayed in his teaching, or the Arian gathered, or the Patripassian taught, or the Homuncionite falsely claimed, or the Cataphrygian urged, or the Borborite seized upon. These we condemn with a catholic mouth that believes in Christ God, together with all who follow or teach them or wish to assert them. All their dogmas we dissolve among ourselves by the light of the divine testimonies, not that we are sufficient to think anything of ourselves, as coming from ourselves; our sufficiency is from God.
Among these, however, is a new saying, damnable not only in deed, I would say, but even in the telling, and not

put forward by any heretical author before this. Ithacius read it out and brought this sacrilegious abomination to our ears: that the tasting of first fruits ought to be either expiated or consecrated by magical incantations, and that an accursed ointment should be consecrated to the Sun and the Moon, along with which it will perish. Whoever has read, put forward, believed, done, held or introduced this is not only anathema maranatha but must also be pursued with the sword, since it is written: "You shall not allow sorcerers to live." So let the heretics keep for themselves their wicked inventions and interpretations worthy of Gehenna; let the schismatics keep for themselves the shifting wishes of their slander: no one will tear down the tabernacle of Christ God and the temple that is within us. Let them, reading the scriptures, think that God is made of rock, of horn, of stone. For us, in all scripture, as it is written, God is the unicorn; for us Christ is the rock; for us Jesus is the cornerstone; for us Christ is the man of men. Let them, as children of perdition and of the devil, believe that they are filled with the devil's rain. For us there is the almighty God, who calls the water of the sea and pours it out over the face of the whole earth, and grants the morning and the evening rain.

And if the wretches themselves want to know what kind of god theirs is, the one they believe in: he is, as it is written in the prophet, the beast that sleeps under every tree, among the forest, the papyrus and the rushes. He is the one of whom it is written in Job, where the Lord speaks: "Around his teeth is terror; his innards are shields of bronze, and his binding is like emery stone; no breath will pass through him. When he sneezes, brightness flashes forth; his eyes are like the morning star. Out of his mouth go burning lamps and a ball of fire; his nostrils breathe out the smoke of a furnace of blazing fire; his breath is flames of coals, and blazes come forth from his tongue. In his neck strength abides, and before him runs destruction." He is, as the prophet also says elsewhere, the one who counts rock as stubble and laughs at the earthquake. His bed is sharp stakes, and all the gold there is lies beneath him like the sea, like mud. He makes the deep boil like a bronze cauldron and regards the sea as a mirror, and the Tartarus of the abyss as an eternal captive. Nothing has been made like him on earth

to be mocked by my angels; he looks upon everything lofty, and he is king of all that are in the waters. But for us God is Christ Jesus, who said: "Everything under heaven is mine." He, the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, appeared in the midst of the golden lampstands like a son of man, clothed in a robe reaching to the feet and girded at the breasts with a golden sash. The hair of his head was white as wool and as snow, and, as it is written, his eyes were like a flame of fire, his feet like fine bronze drawn from the furnace, and his voice like the sound of many waters. In his right hand he holds seven stars, from his mouth comes a sword sharp on both edges, and his face is like the sun shining in its strength. This is he who holds the keys of death and of hell; this is he whose name is written on a new white stone, which no one has except the one who has received it. For we give the schismatics no cause for offense if we read the name "God" inscribed on the new stone, for he, in every script, whether Hebrew or Latin or Greek, in everything that is seen or spoken, is King of kings and Lord

of lords. Although the title of the cross was set up in these languages, it nonetheless spells out a divine testimony to God, as do the prophets of God too. So Jeremiah, setting out the characters of the Hebrew alphabet, wept in his laments, and David exulted in the psalms, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess to God. For he is the one of whom it is written: "The lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered." But for us God is not a lion; rather, as it is written, "What is sweeter than honey, and what is stronger than a lion?" He is the one of whom it is written: "Let the stag of friendship and the foal of graces converse with you." But for us God is not a stag or a foal; rather, as it is written, "Before you say, 'Lord, Lord,' he says, 'Here I am,'" and as elsewhere, "Out of the mouths of sucklings you have prepared praise." He is the one who, as it is written in the prophet, alone is able to bind the chain of the Pleiades and unlock the enclosures of Orion. Knowing the changes of the firmament, and destroying the wheel of birth, he has overcome the day of our nativity by the renewal of baptism. He is the one whose name made a way in the sea and a most firm path in the waves,

and to whose name the blaze of the furnace yielded, overcome. Even Balaam, a worshipper of idols and demons, prophesied of him, bearing witness against his own wretchedness, when he said: "A man shall come forth from the seed of Judah and shall rule over many nations, and his kingdom shall be exalted; for the Lord God brought him out of Egypt. His horns are like the glory of the unicorn; he shall devour the nations of his enemies and suck the marrow from their elbows, and with his darts he shall strike his enemies. He shall lie down at rest and be refreshed like a lion and like a lion's whelp; who has roused him? Those who bless him are blessed, and those who curse him are cursed." Because of what he was, no one would accept his words among the prophecies of the righteous. Yet scripture judged it wrong to bar from the Lord's scriptures and condemn whatever even such people prophesied in witness to Christ God, as it is written: "Since wickedness is cowardly, when it is condemned it bears witness to God," and elsewhere: "You believe that God is one; the demons do this too, and they shudder." And if they wish to know what the name is that has lent the working of its power to every mighty work and every tongue,

it is this: Christ Jesus. As it is written: "Gold and silver I do not have; but what I have, I give you: in the name of Jesus, rise and walk." As also elsewhere: "I am the Lord God, this is my name; my glory I will not give to another." And elsewhere John says: "And his garment was sprinkled with blood, and his name was called the Word of God." And elsewhere: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel, which is interpreted, God with us." Turn back, then, at last, wretched schismatic, turn back, and stand in dread of the name of the Lord, which even the whole nature of wild beasts and animals has feared. For it is written: "Offenses must come, but woe to the one through whom they come"; and: "Would that you were either hot or cold; but since you are lukewarm, you will be spewed out of the Lord's mouth." But, as it is written, take counsel with yourself, repent, and buy yourself gold refined by fire. Then, having become what you have bought, like gold purged by fire, you will have the name of the Lord, which is Jesus, written on you, when by repenting of what you do you show forth the name of the Lord the Savior, because it is through him that you will have been saved. For it is written:

"And his name shall be called Jesus, for he it is who will save all the people"; and: "Understand parables and dark sayings, the words of the wise and their riddles." For mighty is he who said: "When you turn back and groan, then you will be saved." From the beginning our God saved his people in many and various ways, as he showed in deed to our fathers, and he made this manifest when he came in the flesh, called by the name Jesus. But if anyone thinks otherwise, he will bear the judgment, whoever he is. Let them, as the wretches say, regard God as male-female. For us, however, the Spirit of God is in both men and women, as it is written: "God made man in his image and likeness; male and female he made them, and he blessed them." As the apostle also says of him: "Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God." And since we are his men, and he is the man and our head, the apostle promised that he would present us, betrothed in faith, as a chaste virgin to one husband, for there is neither male nor female, but we are all one in Christ Jesus. So let everything they read be confusion for them; for us let it be instruction, to understand what is written and to know the power of the living word.

We must not judge the nature of the divine word with a wandering, fleshly mind, through the confusing images of carnal lusts. Rather, as it is written, the invisible things of God can be known from the creation of the world through the things that have been made. For these are the ones who, wearing the stained tunic of the flesh, have turned the grace of the divine word into lust. They despise dominions, blaspheme dignities, scorn prophecies and deny the resurrection, as it is written: going more and more after the desires of the flesh, they despise piety, hardened in their audacity, and because of their unanimity, since [?], they do not fear to blaspheme, and destruction does not slumber for them. But we know that there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved except Christ Jesus. For us, neither Armaziel nor Mariame nor Joel nor Balsamus nor Barbilon is God, but Christ Jesus, of whom it is written: "And let all the angels of God worship him." He it is who makes his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire, and who is fulfilled all in all. He is the promised seed, ordained through angels

by the hand of a mediator. He it is who is above every principality and power and might and dominion, and above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come. He is our God, and no other shall be reckoned besides him. He is head over the whole church, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all things in all. Whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas, or the world or life or death, or things present or things to come: all are ours, and we are Christ's, and Christ is God's.

And this is the one judgment of all of us. Whatever is put forward as said by anyone, under whatever name, whether prophets or apostles or angels: if it prophesies or preaches Christ as God, speaks of God according to Moses, the prophets and the gospels while condemning the vices of the world, and agrees with the catholic faith, we embrace it. But if, wickedly, it denies that Jesus is God, dissents from Moses, the gospels or the prophets, and urges the sacrileges of wretched dogmas, which is not lawful, then it is neither prophet nor apostle nor angel, even if it bears a holy name, but we hold it as anathema and a deserter,

as it is written that no one speaking in the Holy Spirit says "Jesus be anathema," and no one except in the Holy Spirit calls Jesus Lord. As John also says: "Every spirit that confesses that Christ Jesus has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God, and this is the antichrist." As he also says elsewhere: "Those who do not confess that Christ Jesus came in the flesh, these are deceivers and antichrists." So too Joshua son of Nun, the Lord's prophet and leader in Israel, when an angel appeared to him, trusted not in the appearance alone but in the words of confession, and cried out to the angel: "Are you ours or our adversaries'?" And the angel, so that his words might be believed, confessed that he was commander of the Lord's army. And so Joshua, who believed in nothing apart from God, then gave credence to the words of the angel speaking to him, since he had not denied that he belonged to the Lord's army. So too the apostle John in the Apocalypse, when he wished to worship the angel who was speaking to him, was shown that God must be worshipped, not angels, for the angel said to him: "Do not do it, John; for I am your fellow servant and that of your brothers who hold the testimony. Worship Jesus rather, as God!"
"For the testimony of Jesus is also the spirit of prophecy." As Isaiah also says: "Neither a messenger nor an angel, but the Lord himself will come and save us."

But if some, puffed up and knowing nothing, invent or confess some fifth gospel beyond the four gospels, why is this brought forward to stir up ill will against us, who reject the wretched follies of such people? For these are the ones in whom the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so that the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God, may not shine in them. May all the wrath of the Lord come upon anyone who writes this in titles, or confesses or believes it. But we, having entered the body of the venerable church of God through the creed, have come to know an indissoluble faith, watered from one threefold spring, in the arrangement of the four gospels. We believe that there is no other God but Christ God, the Son of God, who was crucified for us and revealed in his name the baptism of remission. From the beginning of the world he predestined his elect in prophecy, from whom came Christ according to the flesh, just as the Lord's genealogy in the gospel is preserved, set out and declared through them; and through them the Lord, prophesying himself, prepared the way for his coming. As it is written: "I will pour out my spirit

upon all flesh, and their sons and daughters shall prophesy, their young men shall see visions, and their old men shall dream dreams. Even upon my servants and my handmaids I will pour out my spirit, and I will show wonders in the heaven above and signs on the earth below. The sun shall be turned to darkness and the moon to blood, before the great day of the Lord comes. And it shall be that whoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved." In this, we too do not despair of speaking about him, for he did not forbid or cut off anyone's spirit, nor did he shut prophecy within a fixed limit; instead he granted that all who believe in him might speak freely about him. As it is also written in the gospel: "Blessed be God, who has visited his people and wrought their redemption, and has raised up a horn in the house of David, as he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets who have been from of old." As the prophet Tobit also says to his son: "We are children of the prophets. Noah was a prophet, and Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and all our fathers who have prophesied from the beginning of the world." As the apostle Jude also says: "Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied of these, saying: 'Behold, the Lord comes with his holy thousands to execute judgment.'" And so too the apostle, closing to no one the way of speaking about God, wrote to the peoples to whom he preached:

"You can all prophesy one by one," he says, "so that all may learn and all may be encouraged"; and elsewhere too: "The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets." So whoever believed in Christ God need not despair of prophesying about God, given what God had promised to all his own.

And so, most blessed bishops, if you consider that God and you have been satisfied, now that the heresies and doctrines have been condemned and our faith clearly stated, bear witness to the truth: free us from the ill will of malicious slander, and report to your brothers so as to heal what the words of slanderers have troubled. For the reward of life is to be approved by those who seek the faith of truth, not by those who, under the name of religious men, pursue private feuds.
THE BOOK OF PRISCILLIAN TO BISHOP DAMASUS.

The catholic faith keeps to the path of the creed given by God, and it seeks the glory of believing rather than of speaking, since what has been brought forth by its own truth needs no clever interpretation; as the Apostle says, "Avoid disputes about the law." Yet the needs of the time compel us, a need forced on us by the injury inflicted on us through Bishop Hydatius. We have always taken the part of patience, and have been eager to bear with anyone rather than to provoke him. Even so, we are glad that things have turned out as they have, so that before you we may speak what we believe. You are the senior of us all, and you came to the glory of the apostolic see nourished by the trials of life, with blessed Peter to encourage you. Before you, then, we fulfil the apostle's faithful word: "With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." In this, having been baptized in Christ and having put on Christ, we confess the faith of truth, sublime indeed in its manifold arrangement yet venerable in the united power of the one God. As we believe it in our heart, so we confess it, for the salvation of all who have been led into stumbling by the false talk of others. For many years ago we were renewed by the regeneration of the living washing, and, rejecting the filthy darkness of worldly

deeds, we gave ourselves wholly to God, for we read that whoever loved anyone more than God could not be his disciple. Some of us had already been chosen for God in the churches, others were labouring in our lives to be chosen, and we were following the quiet of catholic peace. But disputes suddenly arose, whether from necessary rebuke, or from rivalry over manner of life, or from the power of the last times. We longed for the love of Christ our God and for peace, and though we were confident in our conscience, we were nevertheless afraid that strife of minds might bring about something that the peace of the Church could not hold together, as in fact happened. Yet amid all this thanks be to God, who is one and true in all things, that up to this time none of us who have submitted this petition has had either an accuser or a judge able to find his life blameworthy, although to be slandered is not always the lot of the guilty but is sometimes the lot of the peaceable. In fact, at the assembly of bishops held at Saragossa, none of us was held as a defendant; no one was accused, no one convicted, no one condemned. No charge was brought against our name, our way of life or our conduct, and no one had, I will not say the obligation, but even the worry of being summoned.

Some memorandum or other was presented there by Hydatius which set down, as it were, a rule for how life should be lived. None of us was censured there in any of it, above all because your letter prevailed against the wicked, the letter in which, in keeping with the commands of the Gospel, you had directed that nothing be decreed against people who were absent and unheard. Nevertheless, although we were absent there, we have always urged in the churches, and still urge, that wicked conduct, unseemly rules of living and whatever fights against the faith of Christ our God should be condemned out of love for an upright and Christian life. We urge too that no one be forbidden, if he despises parents, children, wealth, rank and even his own life, and chooses to love God rather than the world. Nor should hope of pardon be taken from those who, if they cannot attain the first rank, at least stand in the second or third. For since there are many mansions with God the Father, the hope set before us in Christ must be held by those who keep the faith of the creed uncorrupted, even if they lack the ability to fulfil the perfect work. In this we follow the apostle Paul, who said that he instructed some by command, admonished others by concession, and shaped others by counsel without the authority of a precept, so that he might win all who had come to the faith of Christ by the various calls of mercy.

As for the faith, we hold it and hand it on just as we received it. We believe in one God, the Father almighty, as it is written: "From whom are all things, and we through him"; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, as it is written: "Through whom are all things, and we through him"; born of the Virgin Mary by the Holy Spirit, as it is written: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel, which is interpreted, God with us"; and again concerning him: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High has overshadowed you, and therefore the holy one to be born will be called the Son of God"; who suffered under Pontius Pilate and was crucified, as it is written: "And he will be counted among the wicked"; who was buried and rose on the third day, as it is written in the prophets: "Wait for me on the day of my resurrection"; who ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty, as it is written: "Behold, I saw the heavens opened and the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of God"; who will come from there and judge the living and the dead, as it is written: "He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven." We believe in the holy Church, the Holy Spirit and saving baptism, as it is written: "Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not ascend into the kingdom of heaven."

We believe in the forgiveness of sins, as it is written: "I say to you, little children, that your sins are forgiven you for his name's sake." We believe in the resurrection of the flesh, as it is written: "Even Moses announced the resurrection to come, when the Lord said, 'I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob.' He is not the God of the dead but of the living, for all live to him."

Keeping to the path of this creed, we condemn with a catholic mouth all heresies, doctrines, practices and teachings that have become matters of dispute through partisan zeal rather than through understanding. We have been baptized, as it is written, "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." It does not say "in the names," as of many, but in one, because one God, venerable in threefold power, Christ, is all and in all, as it is written: "The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. It does not say 'and to seeds,' as of many, but as of one, 'and to your seed,' which is Christ." Speaking of this the prophet says: "This is our God, and no other shall be reckoned beside him, who received the law and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. Afterwards he was seen on earth and lived among men."

It would take long to go through each point, and it is repugnant to Christian minds even to repeat the teachings of such wretched people. We say these things before your venerable reverence, however, so that if we fall into what we condemn, we may be condemned by the very profession made in our petition. Who with catholic ears can believe the abomination of the Arian heresy? Its followers divide what is one and want many gods, and so defile the light of the prophetic word. They do not read what Moses said: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one God." The Lord bore witness to him in the Gospel, saying: "What Moses wrote, he wrote about me." Photinus, a kinsman in this wretchedness, refuses to hold what is read: "Cursed is the man who puts his hope in man." Our God himself spoke of this to the man he had healed of his infirmity, and showed what he wished to be believed about himself, saying: "Go and tell how much God has done for you"; and this testimony is true. Who could bear the Patripassian heretics, when Scripture says: "Whoever believes in the Son has life; whoever does not believe in the Son does not have life"? Their wretchedness is so great that they are condemned even by the confession of a demon, for in the Gospel the demon says to God: "What have we to do with you,

Jesus, Son of the living God? Why have you come before the time to destroy us?" What fool would fall in with the Ophites and want to have a serpent for God, when it is written: "I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the house of slavery. You shall have no other gods besides me. You shall not make for yourself an idol or any likeness of what is in heaven above or on earth below or under the waters or under the earth"? Who would want the repeated baptisms of the Novatianists, when it is written: "One faith, one baptism, one God"? With God Christ as our witness, we know the wretchedness of these sects from common talk, not from any exchange in debate, because even to have argued with them is a sin. We know this one thing: those who take for themselves the name of a sect lose the name of Christian. Among all these we condemn the Manichaeans, who are no longer heretics but idolaters and sorcerers, servants of the Sun and Moon, demons of the Unconquered [?], together with all their founders, sects, customs, practices, books, teachers and disciples, because of them it is written: "With such a one do not even eat." For to us, who have been baptized according to the faith of the creed and chosen for the priesthood in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, Christ, God, the Son of God, who suffered in the flesh, is our whole faith,
our whole life, our whole worship.

While we were living in this truth of faith and this simplicity, Hydatius returned from the Synod of Saragossa. He reported nothing against us, since he himself had left us in our churches in communion with him, and no one had condemned us, even in our absence, by any rash accusation. But your venerable reverence should know the source of his burning resentment, and of the fury with which he has raged through the whole world and even against the churches. When he returned from the synod and was sitting in the middle of the church, he was formally charged by his own presbyter, and the charge was entered in the church's records. A few days later a petition was also submitted by certain people in our churches, setting out charges worse than those the presbyter had first brought. A great many of his clergy separated themselves from him, declaring that they would not be in communion with a bishop who had not been cleared. When we were approached about this, we wrote a letter to the bishops Hyginus and Symposius, whose lives you yourself know, to this effect: that everything had suddenly been thrown into confusion, and that steps must be taken to make the restored peace of the churches last. The reply came, to quote its very words: as far as the laity were concerned,

if they held Hydatius under suspicion, it would be enough for them to declare their catholic profession before us; for the rest, a council should be granted for the peace of the churches; but no one had been condemned at the Synod of Saragossa. Who would not believe his fellow bishops, especially since Symposius, the devout man who wrote this, had been present at that very synod? Meanwhile, however, we decided to go to the city of Mérida and see Hydatius in person, as God is our witness, to bring about peace rather than strife. If it was an injury rather than a courtesy to want to consult him face to face as a brother rather than to summon him as a defendant, then we are guilty. But when we came and entered the church, the crowds and people were stirred up against us, and we were not only refused admission to the presbytery but were even beaten. So we think the injury was done by the one who struck, not by those who were struck.

Since peace was dear to our hearts, we accepted the profession of the laity, which we could not reject because it was catholic. We wrote to almost all our fellow bishops about what priestly dignity had suffered, sending also the record of the proceedings and the creed of the professions, and we did not hide the fact that many of those who had made the profession were being sought for the priesthood. The reply came that a council should be granted on these matters; that the profession made should be believed; and that, just as the consecration of a priest rests with a bishop, so the choice by petition rests with the people. Then Hydatius, more afraid than he needed to be, put together a petition, weaving a false tale of what had happened. Without naming us, he sought a rescript against pseudo-bishops and Manichaeans, and of course obtained it, since no one who heard of pseudo-bishops and Manichaeans could fail to hate them. He also told a whole tissue of lies to that eminent man, your brother Bishop Ambrose. When the rescript was brought back to him, he used the name of a sect which every one of us condemns as cover to rush against

all Christians, even calling Hyginus a heretic along with us, as the letters he sent to the churches proclaim. Evidently he was trying to make sure he would have no judges left, by defaming everyone with one slander or another. We commended our churches to God, and we have brought you their letters of communion, sent with the signatures of the whole clergy and people. Those of us who could came to you. We had indeed wished, while still absent, to petition that, if Hydatius had any charge to bring, [?] we might ask for a hearing before bishops, though without shrinking from a public trial if he preferred that. No one who wishes to be vindicated is afraid to be heard on any matter. Whether it was done out of partisanship or ill will, God will judge, but the quaestor, though he said our requests were just, was slow to reply. Nevertheless, not forgetting that in a matter of faith the judgment of the saints is to be preferred to that of the world, we came to Rome, a burden to no one, wishing only to come to you first, so that our silence would not be taken for fear arising from a guilty conscience,

but rather so that, submitting our petition, we might set out the course of events and, what matters more than anything, the catholic faith in which we live. If our opinion is also sought about certain writings which Hydatius brought out of his own book-chest and turned into slanderous tales, our conviction is and always has been this. Whatever is found in writings put forward under the authority of any apostle, prophet or bishop that prophesies or preaches Christ, God, the Son of God, and agrees with the canon, the Gospels or the prophets, cannot be condemned. But whatever thinks or says anything against the canon and against the catholic faith must be condemned along with all its teachers and disciples. For it is written: "Every spirit that confesses Christ is from God, but the one that does not confess him is not from God"; and elsewhere: "No one speaking in the Holy Spirit says 'Jesus is anathema,' and no one says 'Lord Jesus' except in the Holy Spirit." We who are catholics ought not to be condemned if heretics have falsified, to suit themselves, writings that speak of God.

Concerning these writings, Hydatius himself, who does little to clear himself and prefers to use them to defame those he fears will be heard, said this at the Council of Saragossa: "Let what must be condemned be condemned; let what is superfluous not be read." Your reverence can see from this that it is his habit, and not any crime of ours, when people who hold one and the same view are said to hold a different faith. We therefore beg your venerable wisdom to grant us a hearing, since you are senior to all and first among all. We ask this if the faith of our profession stands firm in God according to what you hand on as left to you by the apostles; if the testimonies of our churches, written in letters of peace, are not lacking; if we neither can nor should hold any other view of the Scriptures; and if none of us has been made a defendant, none heard, none deposed in a council, none condemned by proof of any charge brought against him even when he was a layman. We grant that the priesthood is of no help to a guilty man, and that a bishop can be deposed who deserved to be condemned earlier as a layman.

Have Hydatius summoned, and if he is confident he can prove anything against us, let him not lose the crown of the eternal priesthood, provided he pursues zeal for the Lord to the end. Or if, out of your innate kindness, you wish to inflict on no one the injury he has inflicted on us, we beg you to send letters to your brothers the Spanish bishops. For, so as to do injury to no one, we all ask that a council be convened and Hydatius summoned, and that those whom they have read were made defendants in their absence should not be judged without a hearing [?]. Yet let no one condemn except on condition that Hydatius proves everything he alleged in the letters he sent, and let him bear only the burden of proving his accusation. Let him set aside any fear of being found guilty himself, since none of us accuses him. We readily forgive the sin committed against us if we are vindicated, for we know, and learn from our own experience, what befits bishops. We ask only that, once our faith and life have been proved, we may contest the rescript issued against the Manichaeans,

with the testimony of the bishops who take part in the council, so that in your days, under the name of guilty men, the churches may not be bereft of catholic bishops, nor bishops of their churches, which you know would be a wicked thing.
THE BOOK OF PRISCILLIAN ON FAITH AND ON THE APOCRYPHA.

[?] … let him condemn, since novelty of mind is the mother of contention, learning the author of offence, the food of schism, the nourishment of heresy, the very pattern of sin and transgression. For everything that is seen to have been said or done by God or by the apostles, or approved by them to be done, is that of which it is written: "Yes, yes; no, no." But whatever is newly devised by cleverness and slander, here the testimony of the divine power shows itself, which says: "Whatever goes beyond this comes from evil." Let us see, then, whether the apostles of Christ Jesus, the teachers of our way of life and conduct, read nothing outside the canon. The apostle Jude cries out — that twin of the Lord, who, though he is thought to have tested God the Christ after the marks of the passion, believed all the more; who both saw and touched the deep prints of the nails and the glories of the divine cross. "Of these," he says, "Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied, saying: 'Behold, the Lord comes with his holy thousands to execute judgment and to convict all, and concerning all the harsh things that sinners have spoken against him.'" Who is this Enoch whom the apostle Jude took up as a witness to prophecy? Did someone who had prophesied about God have no one else to cite, that he must set down the prophecy of this man — a prophecy which, if what they say is true, he himself would have condemned by the canonical ordinance?

Or perhaps Enoch did not deserve to be a prophet — he who, as Paul testifies in the Epistle to the Hebrews, received testimony before his translation; he whom God, at the beginning of the human race, when the shape of the world and the nature of that raw age, still holding fast the sin of deceived man, did not believe in a future turning to God after sin, chose to translate among his own rather than let perish? If there is no doubt about him, and the apostles are believed when they say he is a prophet, how can it be called deliberation rather than uproar, counsel rather than rashness, faith rather than faithlessness, when a sentence aimed at avenging private grudges condemns a prophet who proclaims God? Or are we dealing with trivial matters? Are knucklebones and dice in our hands, or are we handling the farces of the stage, that we should follow the men of this world and condemn the sayings of the apostles? Or what kind of grace is it, in the name of establishing peace, for men to believe what they please and not keep to the apostolic sayings? But perhaps someone will pride himself on such clever arguments as to say that, although even a single testimony is enough to confirm the faith of the saints in God,

one should nevertheless not believe a thing on a single witness, but that the account of every word stands on two or three witnesses. Let anyone of this sort, then, turn around and, as a careful searcher of the Scriptures, inquire whether we speak the truth. What does it mean that holy Tobit, setting out for his son the precepts of the life to come and declaring what he should keep, said: "We are the sons of prophets; Noah was a prophet, and Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all our fathers who prophesied from the beginning of the world"? When was a book of the prophet Noah read in the canon? Who has read a book of Abraham among the prophets of the established canon? Who has taught that Isaac ever prophesied? Who has heard of a prophecy of Jacob placed in the canon? If Tobit read them and earned the testimony of prophecy in the canon, how is it that what is granted to him as testimony to proven virtue is charged against others as grounds for just condemnation? In all this let each and every one forgive us if we would rather be condemned with the prophets of God than join those who rashly presume in condemning what is holy. For who would not fear Noah as his accuser at the hearing of the divine judgment? Of him the apostle says:

"He preserved Noah, the righteous herald of righteousness, when he brought a flood upon the world of the ungodly." Who would not seek the bosom of the prophet Abraham as the pledge of rest? Who would not wish to be reckoned among the seed of Isaac? Who would not love Jacob, called by God the god of Pharaoh? Or who, spurning the memorials of the saints, would not tremble, since it is written: "Truly I tell you, whoever causes one of the least of these who have believed in my name to stumble, it would be better for him to have a great millstone tied around him and be thrown into the depths of the sea"? If this is said of the least, I would like to know what is pronounced concerning those who are first in the faith. Yet in all these books there is no reason to fear deleting whatever has been inserted by the wretched heretics, and rejecting whatever is not found to agree with the prophets or the Gospels. For those holy men of God themselves do not embrace a lie among truths, or sacrilegious and detestable things in place of holy ones. It is better to pull the darnel out of the crop than to lose the hope of good fruit because of the darnel, which the devil sowed with his own among the holy things for this very purpose: that, unless there were a careful reaper, the crop would perish with the darnel and he would make the good die with the worst,

binding under one and the same sentence both the one who joins the worst with the good and the one who destroys the good along with the bad. Moreover, in the Gospel according to Luke, God testifies through the evangelist, saying: "The blood of all the prophets shed since the foundation of the world will be required, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who was killed between the altar and the sanctuary." And Elijah says in the book of Kings: "They have dug down your altars, they have killed your prophets, and I alone am left, and they seek my life." Who is this prophet Abel, from whom the blood of the prophets took its beginning, a line that begins with him and ends with Zechariah? Who are those in between who are understood to have been killed? For if everything that is said must be looked for in the books of the canon, and to have read more is a sin, we read of no prophet killed among those placed in the canon. And if nothing outside the authority of the canon may be taken up or held, then we cannot simply believe in fables without holding to a written history confirmed by proof of the events. Perhaps someone will jump up and say that Isaiah was sawn in two. If there is such a person among those who have condemned these writings,

let him shut his mouth, or else, when he brings forward the history of that event, let him admit that he believes paintings or poets — since people nowadays more readily accept what the studies of the philosophers invent — so long as there is testimony of such a thing and the blood of the prophets killed since the foundation of the world may be required. If the evangelist, having read these things, rightly brought them forward as testimony, saying "Search the Scriptures," he has drawn me too to read what he had read. And I cannot say what I am being forced to say: that following the apostle was for me not instruction in the faith but the snare of a man deceived. For again in the Gospel according to Matthew it stands written: "Joseph rose and took the child and his mother by night and went into Egypt, and remained there until the death of Herod, so that what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled: 'Out of Egypt I have called my son.'" Who is this prophet, whom we do not read in the canon, whose prophecy the Lord fulfilled faithfully, as a guarantor makes good a promised gift? Surely it is no small undertaking that was granted: to believe that God would suffer, and by the testimonies of prophecy to prepare, as it were,

the road of the divine journey, from which God would not turn aside, so as to prove that he had spoken in the one who had prophesied. Surely a book cannot be condemned whose testimony fulfils the trustworthiness of the canonical utterance. Nor can one thing be chosen and another rejected as though among the whims of mortal banquets; nor is this a question of sophistries, where each follows whatever he has taken up, and where, wanting a dialectical exercise of wits, they have made sects out of mere persuasion. The Scripture of God is a solid thing, a true thing, not chosen by man but handed down to man from God; and if the firstfruits are holy, the whole lump is holy too. This, in short, is where heresy comes from: each one serves his own wit rather than God, and they set out not to follow the creed but to dispute about the creed, whereas if they knew the faith they would hold nothing outside the creed. For the creed is the seal of a true thing, and to break the seal of the creed is to prefer disputing about the creed to believing it. The creed is the work of the Lord, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit: faith in one God, from whom Christ — God, the Son of God, the Savior — was born in the flesh, suffered, and rose again for love of mankind. Handing the creed to his apostles, he who was, is, and was to come showed in himself and in his creed the name of the Father as the Son, and likewise the name of the Son as the Father,

and taught this so that the error of the Binionites should not prevail. For when the apostles asked him, he showed that he was all that was named, and he willed to be believed as one, not divided, as the prophet says: "This is our God, and no other shall be reckoned besides him, who showed the way of discipline and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved; afterward he was seen on earth and lived among men; the Lord God is his name." But lest we be accused of having turned, out of love for the faith, to matters other than those we set out to treat — although there is abundant room for overcoming the various heresies — we want the work we have undertaken to deal specifically with this point: to overcome faithless falsehood with a cloud of testimonies. Now we must return to those matters, so that, if we are found commendable on the point for which we are criticized, we may be seen to have argued rightly about the rest as well. Thus Paul says that God said: "It is more blessed to give than to receive," and we do not read in the canon that God said this. And Daniel testifies that God spoke, saying: "For iniquity shall come forth from Babylon, from elders who seemed to govern the people."

And while we used to believe these things done, said, or written — in the words of the evangelist, in the speech of the apostle, and in the divine discourses — behold, a time has now come when, as a dispute over superfluous matters is pursued, bewilderment is sown among the faithful. For we cannot say that God did not say what the apostle said he said, or that what Scripture testifies a prophet said was never prophesied. And while we rightly believe these things as matters of faith, we do not see them written in the canon. Therefore, if everything outside the canon is to be condemned, either how is the testimony of condemned writings accepted, or else the authority of the writer is not upheld in what he has written. So too the prophet Ezekiel says: "Thus says the Lord to Gog: 'You are the one of whom I spoke in ancient days through the hands of my servants the prophets.'" I believe that he said it, and I am not so faithless to myself as to affirm either that the prophet invented what God said or that God lied. Yet who that prophet was through whom God said this I do not see in the canon; and though we have faith in the sayings, we do not find their author written in the canon.

Likewise in the books of Chronicles we find the prophet Nathan, Ahijah the Shilonite, the visions of Iddo, and the words of Jehu son of Hanani cited to vouch for the truth and to give authority to what was done, as Scripture says: "And the rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, first and last, behold, they are written in the words of Jehu son of Hanani, who recorded the kings of Israel in a book." We do not read these writings in the books of the canon, but we find them approved by the canon. As it also says there: "And the rest of the acts of Solomon, first and last, behold, they are written in the words of Nathan the prophet, and in the words of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the visions of Iddo, which he saw concerning Jeroboam son of Nebat." And again there: "And the rest of the acts of Rehoboam, first and last, and all his deeds, are they not written in the words of Shemaiah the prophet and of Iddo the seer?" And again there: "And the rest of the acts of Abijah, his deeds and his words, are written in the book of the prophet Iddo." And again there: "And the rest of the acts of Amaziah, first and last, behold, are they not written in the book of the days of the kings of Judah and Israel?"
