Again there: "Are these not written in the book of the days of the kings of Judah?" Again there: "And the rest of the acts of

Manasseh, and his prayer which he prayed to the Lord in the name of the God of Israel, behold, they are written in the words of his prayer and in the words of the seers." Who, then, could patiently endure such a tossing of waves? On one side unlearned madness presses us, ignorant fury makes its demands, saying nothing but: "Are the things you say catholic or not? Condemn what I do not know, condemn what I do not read, condemn what in my zeal for sluggish idleness I do not look into." On the other side the divine word presses us: "Search the Scriptures," it says, warning us in particular that the words of those whose blood is required as testimony [?] must not be denied. Placed between these, we are now of necessity resolved to make confidence of what we earlier called caution. I have the testimony of God, I have that of the apostles, I have that of the prophets. If I seek what belongs to a Christian man, what belongs to the order of the Church, what belongs to God the Christ, I find it in those who preach God, I find it in those who prophesy. It is not fear but faith that makes us love the better and reject the worse, keeping one rule in all this: since in books of this kind —

which diligence retained for the labour of reading outside the number of the canonical books, and which were taken up to confirm what we read written in the canon — the mind of the heretics has invaded many of them and, preparing war against Catholics, has preferred to falsify them rather than keep them intact, we should rightly apply that apostolic rule: every spirit that denies Jesus is not of God, and every spirit that confesses Christ Jesus is of God, as it is written: "For no one speaking in the Holy Spirit says 'Jesus is accursed,' and no one says 'Jesus is Lord' except in the Holy Spirit." Indeed, in the ancient records of the books, when the devil begrudged the testament of the Scriptures, it was not enough for him that Jerusalem was taken, the altar of the Lord defiled, and the temple destroyed. For since it was easy for man to restore with his hands what had been made with hands, the ark of the testament was burned, the devil knowing that human nature, bound to the world, would easily lose its faith if it did not have the testimonies of the Scriptures for the proclamation of the divine name. But the nature of the divine mystery is shrewder than the devil's: to show what God could do in a man, it willed that Ezra be preserved, who wrote out again what had been burned. If we believe that these were truly burned and truly rewritten, then although the burning of the testament is read in the canon,

and its rewriting by Ezra is not read in the canon, nevertheless, since the testament could not have been restored after it was burned unless it had been written again, we rightly give credence to that book which, brought forth with Ezra as its author, though not placed in the canon, is retained with due veneration as testimony to the restoration of the divine testament. In it we read that the Holy Spirit, who holds the deeds of men and of things from the beginning of the world, entered the heart of a chosen man; and that, writing by day and not falling silent by night, he set down for human memory, repeated in order, number, and reckoning, everything that is seen to have been done or that we read in writing — things which the written form could scarcely preserve for human memory. Here one would like to cry out: It is so! Let it be allowed! How, I ask, are we to blame for reading a few of these, when we are more guilty for not reading all that has been prophesied about God? I have no doubt, however, that one of those who love slander rather than faith will say: "Seek nothing further! It is enough for you to read what is written in the canon." I would readily rise to agree with his words, given the bent of human nature, which seeks leisure rather than labour,

were I not pressed by the testimony of Luke the evangelist, who says in the Acts of the Apostles: "The disciples together compared the Scriptures among themselves, to see whether it was so, as Paul had told them." And I recognize that the things I wish to know received the testimony of prophecy in the canon. For although it is a crime not to have believed the apostolic words, it is no damnable fault to build the foundation of faith on the proof of writings, and to leave nothing in which the devil's rebuttal could show us weak. For the divine word, since everything it had said was its own, could have spoken as if from itself, not saying that something had been written by another, but uttering it in its own person. But in saying that it was written, it necessarily set before us the duty of reading, and it neglected neither its own glory, which had been prophesied, nor the gratitude owed by posterity to the one who had prophesied. I, for my part, standing between the two, am a debtor to both: I will read the one who prophesied for the remembrance of God, and I will believe God. For who would not delight that Christ was prophesied before the ages, not by a few but by all? Or who is so barren a judge of the divine greatness and of so incredible a miracle — that God should be born [?] and that a virgin's womb should have opened

as a bodily dwelling, in the service of the divine Word, to conceive and to bear — that he would suppose the secrets of the divine mind did not cry out to all the earth and to every man, since it is written: "Let every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father"?

And therefore, whoever it may be who denies these things, I at least know that he will receive the reward of that Pharisee who, when the Lord arrived and the whole crowd together with the apostles was crying out, "Hosanna, hosanna in the heavens, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord," said that those who so unhesitatingly refused to keep silent about the glories of the God present among them ought to be rebuked. But let anyone of this sort note that the Lord said: "Even if these are silent, the stones will cry out," and let him understand: if the hardness of rocks, dead by nature, is brought to life for the use of human speech in order to bear witness to God, how can the tongue of the saints be shut, when it is urged to confess both by its own nature and by divine grace? For if pagan souls, entangled in the images and ceremonies of idols, speak of the swift passages of birds and the wind-borne courses of wings as if they gave foreknowledge of future events, and of the veins of entrails throbbing with the life of an earthly

spirit; if, putting their faith in demons, they assert that the innards of animals about to die in a moment foretell the future, and ask the dead about life, saying to a stone "Arise" and to a piece of wood "Awake"; and if thus among them sacrilege is called devotion and ignorance is named wisdom, while they do not know that they are sacrificing not to God but to a demon — if such men take glory in this among themselves, how can we reject the divine prophecies of the saints and, obeying our own wills, begrudge those who prophesied God, abandoning the apostolic precepts that say: "Do not quench the Spirit, do not despise prophecies"? And therefore, since where there is freedom there is Christ, I wish to cry out one thing on behalf of all, for I too have the Spirit of the Lord: Let the devil's envy cease! The Lord was announced by all, Christ was prophesied by all — by Adam, Seth, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and by the others who prophesied from the beginning of the world. And I say fearlessly what the devil begrudges: every man knew that God would come in the flesh — not to mention those whom God placed in the Gospel in the order of his genealogy, to supply both faith in his divine nature and the number of the canon. Just as for those who know and deny the punishment is greater,

so too it is perfect glory not only to believe with the heart but also not to deny that glory with the mouth of confession, as David says: "I believed, and therefore I spoke." In this the apostle Peter too, knowing the reckoning of the number of the canonical books and granting freedom to read what has been written about Christ, said when he sent the letter to the Colossians: "When this letter has been read among you, see that it is read also in the church of the Laodiceans, and that you read the one from Laodicea." Was the apostle worthy of condemnation in your eyes, then, for allowing his disciples to read a letter that was not in the canon? Or do we care more for Christ than he did, and do you so follow your own wills that you extend an unjust judgment even to things decreed before your time? For to all of us who believe that Christ is God, the fullness of faith is the day of the Lord, and the law of life is the pattern of the apostolic precept. Since faith comes from hearing, and hearing stands firm through faith, how is the hope of things to come set before us if what was taught beforehand — written or spoken about Christ, kept in memory, never rejected by the apostles but read by them — is not only spurned by us but condemned as sacrilegious, when it is written in the Gospel:

"Whoever does a mighty work in my name cannot speak evil of me"? In this, however, I do not refuse or reject the view that these things should not be entrusted to untrained ears, lest — since many of them have been falsified by heretics — while seeking a divine work in the words of the saints under the title of the prophets' names, they fall into the pit of heretical falsehood, not holding fully to the discipline of the apostolic word. But neither should the prophecy of the saints be condemned because of the wickedness of the worst. For in all the heresies they have built the institutions of their wretched sects out of a perverse interpretation of all the Scriptures, and all of them affirm that they believe Christ is God and that they are Christians. Yet divine Scripture is not therefore to be condemned, nor the faith of Christ rejected, nor the name of Christian shunned, just because, in trying to assert their sacrileges, they dare to usurp a share in the catholic name.

For if we choose to condemn everything they read, we surely condemn even what is included in the canon. It is better, then, to condemn a deadly interpretation and a sacrilegious teaching than divine Scripture, since it is written: "To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the rest I will speak in parables, so that seeing they may not see and hearing they may not hear." To me, certainly, a servant of the Lord, considering these things, there is this single conviction: whoever does not love Christ, let him be anathema, maranatha.
PRISCILLIAN'S EASTER TREATISE

Nature itself teaches us that, among the uncharted ways of human life and the world's petty struggles, which are unworthy of God, nothing is more useful to a person than to reject every day the things that are friendly to the world and to keep the precepts of God's teaching. As the apostle says: "All friendship with the world is enmity with God"; and again the prophet says: "Do not delay to turn to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day." Even so, the minds of mortals, held captive by their familiarity with worldly things, are shut up within the error of human weakness. Yet amid so many rash courses, God's mercy always comes to meet those in danger of shipwreck, as if of their end, as a harbor and a longed-for port. Taking up through the voices of the prophets the one measure of the divine decree, God appointed the glorious day of the Pasch. He wanted his people to serve him every day. But the whole world lies in the power of the evil one, and since there is no end to things that have no limit, we set no measure to uncertain things by planting our step firmly on slippery ground. Therefore,

by urging us to commemorate the passion he underwent for us, he would at least once a year compel us to the obedience of faith, mindful that we owe him alone the whole of our life. As the apostle says: "Whether death or life or things present or things to come, all are yours, and you are Christ's, and Christ is God's."

And so, dearly beloved in God, we have been placed here to set your minds free, hemmed in as they are by the narrow limits of human weakness, and to bring them into a new light by the devout encouragement of our teaching. It is therefore necessary that, as the forty days of Lent begin in preparation for receiving Easter, we act "as good stewards of the manifold grace of God," as it is written. Some things we forbid by command, and others we ask of you as a concession. At this season the one who already keeps away from evil and is growing used to the good should want what is better. The one who is still bound by the undisciplined error of the world is urged to be called back from what is foreign to him, at least by observing the holy days. Then, when the Lord's Pasch comes, the believer may rejoice

that he has kept the faith of the commandments he once received, the penitent may regain salvation, and the catechumen may not lose confidence in the forgiveness to come. So what is written will be fulfilled: "Behold the day of the Lord and his salvation! Open the gates, so that a people that keeps justice and truth may enter, for those who embrace understanding have received peace, hoping in the Lord." For this reason, dearly beloved, you who share in the heavenly calling, make your souls chaste for God. As it is written, abstain from the bodily desires that wage war against you in your members [?]. When you fast for God, do not fast amid shameful gain, or the uncertainty of greed, or amid quarrels [?] and strife. In these days God's work does ask for abstinence from delicacies and the hardening of the body, but it does not ask for that kind of fast. Instead, as it is written, be chaste in body and spirit, and show a charity that is simple in love and comes from a true heart. Show yourselves rich in good works for the divine glory. As the prophet says, loose every bond of injustice and reject the obligations of oppressive dealings.

Rescue the one who suffers wrong, defend the orphan, do justice for the widow, set the broken free, and tear up every unjust contract. Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the needy and the homeless into your houses. If you see the naked, clothe them, and do not despise those who are in distress. For it is written: "If you give your bread to the hungry from your heart and satisfy the afflicted soul, your light will rise in the darkness, your God will be with you, and you will be filled with every good thing your soul desires." Consider what the Lord's Pasch is. The apostle says: "Christ, our Pasch, has been sacrificed," and so he shows that bearing present things patiently leads on to the reward of blessed immortality. In the Pasch there is the Virgin's childbearing. In taking a body, almighty God did not refuse the shame of a human beginning. He bore in himself manifold proofs of his reality and so rebuked the faults of human birth.

In conception, birth, crying and the cradle he passed through all the indignities of our nature. He did this so that, coming in the flesh, he might overturn the ordinance of the earlier decree. He nailed the curses of earthly dominion to the gibbet of the glorious cross, and though he himself was immortal and could not be conquered by death, he died to give eternity to those who die. Some of us have been buried with him through baptism into death, and others long to die with him and be buried with him. We ought therefore to come to Easter Day in this way: since his humiliation is our honor, let us imitate the Lord's forty days of fasting in the desert as told in the gospel, so that while we walk in the flesh we may not live according to the flesh. Then, even if we have been overcome for a little while, we may be restored by the divine light of the commandments to our place in the framework of Christ's body. For as one who has obtained mercy, I am your counselor, and I am a witness that we cannot be free from sins unless we are saved by the forgiveness of baptism and the redemption of the divine cross.

These are the days in which Moses fasted for forty days and was found worthy to receive the law, the utterance of the divine word. This was when, at the announcement of the Lord's Pasch, the sea was afraid. The mightiest element on earth, whose very nature is storm, parted its waters and gave the people a dusty road. Against its usual way, so as to give the world a miracle, the barren sand brought forth pasture of grass. These are the days which Joshua son of Nun likewise spent in fasting when he entered the land of promise. God's people were clad in the armor of faith, and the ark of the Lord stood in the midst of the waters. Then the Jordan, full to all its banks, gave the people a dry road. Whether it ran down ahead or flowed back behind, it was afraid lest its nature resist the divine command. These are the days which God, coming in the flesh, after he had enriched the font of baptism, spent in the desert, fasting day and night, and overcame. He was tempted by the devil, now through the need of fasting, now through mortal ambition, now through fear. God could not be tempted,

yet he was preparing the passion that would save us and fulfilling in himself the decrees of the Pasch, not abolishing them. By choosing to be tempted, he showed what we ought to reject in these days. And the answers we read that he gave to the devil when he tempted him were given for our faith, so let us use them to destroy the devil's temptation.
PRISCILLIAN'S TRACTATE ON GENESIS.

The form of the prophetic precept took bodily shape in order to proclaim the divine glories. It is held in the lodging of an earthly dwelling, yet it is filled with the light of the Spirit of God, and so it arranges the works of prophecy in such a way that it ascribes present things to God, instils in people the faith to believe, and through the things that are seen shows what spiritual understanding accomplishes in us. Everything that was either done or written is shown to have been spoken to correct people who are falling away and to strengthen the faith of believers. The divine law is set before us, and the power within us is kept for the one God,

so that an end is promised to passing things, punishment to sinners, and eternal things to mortals. As it is written: "The heavens themselves will perish, but you will remain. They will all grow old like a garment, and you will fold them up like a cloak, but you are the same, and your years will not fail." Holy Moses was taught by divine words and chosen for the work of the gospel plan. At his birth he was granted a beginning like that of the One who was to come in the flesh: from the very people who laid snares for his life he received the comforts of being brought up. Later, after Egypt had been struck and God's people set free, he was the first to begin the signs. Joined in fellowship with God and nourished by growing in the divine precepts, he gave the canon its beginning, and he had already displayed its fullness in himself as a testimony, teaching by written words and showing the work of the word in deeds. So it is written of him: "And the Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as one speaks to his friend."

Moses therefore foresaw the doctrines of future heretics and the various notions of those who argue. Some like to think that the world was not made but has always existed, and so, having no beginning, it will be eternal forever. Others flatter themselves in their pleasures. They want to blame all their sins on the malice of the devil or of the world, not on themselves, although it is written: "Ephraim set a stumbling block for himself, loving the Canaanites," and elsewhere the apostle says: "Where do the wars and quarrels among you come from? Do they not come from your own desires?" In this way they accuse the nature of the world. Because they judge it evil, they claim that God made none of the things that appear. They delight in bodily lusts and ascribe the making of their own body to the devil. So they think they do not know what they are doing, and that the sins they commit in their bodies are not subject to the care of God's providence, although it is written: "The body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that ponders many things."

Still others reckon the sun and moon to be gods, though these are lights appointed to serve humanity, and they give the principalities of the world power over the elements, although it is written: "What is brighter than the sun? Yet even it will fail," and elsewhere: "He calls the water of the sea and pours it out over the face of the whole earth; the Lord God almighty is his name." All these people, dearest brothers, are wrapped in the darkness of ignorance. They overthrow those who waver and lead those who agree with them into the dangers of their own ruin. As it is written, they are "clouds without water, carried about by the winds, autumn trees without fruit, dead and uprooted, fierce waves of the sea foaming out their own shame, deceitful stars, for whom storm and the gloom of darkness have been reserved." Their judgment has long been barely enough, and their destruction does not slumber. They do not know that all this that is seen will perish at an end set by God. They do not know that the darkness was given light, and nature was found for creation, for this reason:

so that, divided by the numbering of seasons and days, they might provide a dwelling for people laboring in the work of Christ, and creation might not go beyond what the divine will had established, since it was meant to keep the divine ordinances by serving us. For it is written of such people: "Your father the devil was a liar from the beginning." Whoever has been given a beginning in lying by nature cannot keep to the way of truth. For this reason I urge and warn you: you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ, so cast off the darkness of the world and walk honorably as in the daytime. As the apostle says, let no one plunder you by the philosophy of this world rather than according to Christ. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God, and the things that are seen are mortal, while the things that are not seen are eternal. Pay attention to the meaning of the reading you have heard: "In the beginning God made heaven and earth." Know, then, that God made everything that was made. He fitted the elements together

and stretched out the solid nature of the sky. He gave the use of the air to the powers of the winds, and so, through the fourfold turn of the seasons, he established the course of the year and the order of the stars. When the word of divine power appeared and said, "Let there be light," everything that had been in darkness was laid open. Night was divided at evening from the brightness of light, and each thing was set apart in its place in the appointed order. Then the earth was made firm. The elements were to serve one another in turn, and with the seasons alternating evenly, the earth, given life by the spirit of life, would bring forth the use of the work as it had been arranged. This does not mean that earth or sky, or earthborn principalities produced from related elements, received any spirit with power of its own. Rather, once the matter of things had been prepared, the divine Word entered the work of creation to complete what the precepts of wisdom had established, holding the world's marketplace, which was established as a dwelling for humanity. Finally, when all the things found in the life of the world had been made, each according to its kind, God made man

in his own image and likeness. He took the clay of an earthly dwelling and gave life to our body. He set man over all things as their lord, so that he might place his sabbath, that is, his rest, in the one in whom he had given bodily form to his image and likeness. After that, man would receive a bodily lodging from man by inherited nature, and flesh would be born of flesh. Placed in this condition and following the commands of the divine precepts, flesh made chaste would conquer the work of the world and the nature of earthly matter. Man would make use of the world's service without being deceived by the will of concupiscence. He would have in himself the testimony of the image and likeness of God, and, glorified in the body, he would become a temple of the Lord. Then, when the world had kept sabbath in all things, he would present the rest that he had promised to God within himself.

Finally, our God himself, ordering all things in himself throughout the whole of Scripture, chose to be called by every name that is spoken. He alone has power to save and to destroy, and so in every work of a word that is named he would not withhold punishment from sinners

or glory from those who labor in him. As it is written: "Behold, I lay in Zion a chief cornerstone, chosen, and whoever believes in it will not be put to shame. To you who believe, then, belongs this honor. But for those who do not believe, the stone that the builders rejected has become the head of the corner, a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense. They stumble at the word and do not believe." From this you may understand how the name of a single thing could bring some people growth in faith and bring others offense as the punishment for sin. For he made himself a door for those who enter, the way for those who walk in God's precepts, a fountain of justice for the thirsty, bread for the hungry, and he set himself as a vine for the salvation of believers. As it is written in the gospel: "I am the vine, you are the branches." Whoever recognizes him as all in all gives no share in Christ to any other name or power, and believes in one God, whom he finds to be one in all things. As it is written:

"that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father." As he himself also says through the prophet: "I am God, and before me there was no other, and after me there will be none like me. I am God, and there is no one besides me who saves." Likewise in the same place: "I am the first and I am the last, and besides me there is no God. Who is like me?" Likewise through Jeremiah: "This is our God, and no other will be reckoned beside him. He found the whole way of wisdom and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After this he was seen on earth and lived among men."

So you too, my beloved, make your souls chaste for the obedience of faith. Put off the old self with all its deeds and desires, and put on the new self within you. Through the understanding of spiritual virtues, enter into the work of the reading you have heard, and prepare within yourselves

the Lord's heaven and earth. As it is written: "The heaven of heavens is the Lord's," and elsewhere the Lord says: "Be a willing land for me." Then, when the evening of ignorance has passed away, the cry will go up within you: "Let there be light." As it is written: "Be enlightened, be enlightened, Jerusalem." When the darkness of the corruptible body has been disciplined and you have been ordered by the light of the divine Spirit within you, you will be called the day of the Lord. For whoever does these things in the works of Christ first completes a day in the knowledge of himself. Placed then on the second step, he rightly learns the firmament of all the commandments, so that what was barren in him is made fruitful by the word of the Lord. Receiving the rain of divine preaching, he forms it into every grace of the catholic profession of faith. So he plows in the hope of his faith and gathers its fruits, growing toward the glory of the perfect week and its work, and he forms the Lord's church anew within himself through faith in Christ. As it is written: "Wisdom has built herself a house and founded it on seven pillars." Into that house you too, like living stones,

are being built into spiritual houses, offering spotless sacrifices acceptable to God. You have been born again, not of corruptible seed but of incorruptible, through the word of the living God that abides forever. Having been made the Lord's sabbath and set free from all the business of the world, you will owe nothing to the world, but will rest in Christ.
PRISCILLIAN'S TRACTATE ON EXODUS.

For believers the word of God was indeed enough. Poured into us through the testimony of the apostle, together with the very power of the truth, it taught the meaning of the word spoken in parables when Paul said: “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed.” But the meaning of visible things does not at once grasp how things work, what the times signify, or how to understand the nature that has been ordered within us. And although earthly things cannot be compared with God at all,

all Scripture needs interpretation, and the weakness of human understanding forces us to look to the forms of earthly things as pointers to higher ones. In this way the habits of the visible world can gently remind us and help build up a devout understanding of unfamiliar meanings. For your sake, then, we must stretch our lowly speech to things that seem beyond telling. When something visible is set down in God's law, what is set down is not to be taken for God. All speech [ser = sermo] comes from meaning, so in the manner that speech requires, once the nature of the thing in question is recognized, the understanding mind can put into words for itself what God seeks in us. The first thing you must understand is that all Scripture, in everything it says or speaks, is divided into a threefold work of understanding. Either it destroys the work of the world in us and disciplines the dwelling of earthly flesh in its lusts, as the prophet says: “Chastity will guard and justify the heart”;

or it recalls the divine lineage of the soul and reshapes whatever in us seems bound to days, months, times, desires and the idolatrous vices of earthly birth, as the apostle says: “If we live by the Spirit, let us walk by the Spirit”; or it shows God in man, our daily witness, who suffered for us and is also our judge. Since he willed that we should share in the divine nature, he binds us in body, soul and spirit to a threefold keeping of the commandments. In this way, reformed in spirit through the shadow of the law and trained in cutting away the works of the flesh, we may enter the solemn feast of the heavenly Passover. Raised from death, because Christ died for us out of immortality, we may understand this: he who became all things for us demands for his offerings days, months, kinds of cattle, the natures of animals, different trees and the fruits of earthly seeds. Yet he does not want things that belong to the elements, or earthly things. He shows that all things are his, and what he wants is the purifying of earthly flesh and of the spirit,

and for this reason he himself also suffered for us in the flesh. He demands this as a triumph over the sin that works in us. Speaking his whole self through the nature of all things, he wants the ordinances of the world to be destroyed rather than worshiped, so that what is written may be shown to be true: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand, and became like the beasts.” By the grace of the divine sacrament, the work of the paschal mystery is directed, and the law of the Old Testament is sent ahead, as if building the future road of our salvation. In this way that grace prepares the entrance of God, who was to come into a new light and suffer, and for the preparation of the paschal day it requires a lamb to be slain, and in this it speaks of Christ. The one is called the Passover of the Lord and the other the sacrifice of Christ, and a beast of the earth is very different from the God of glory. The one is earthly, mortal and perishable, given life by the command of a living soul for the use of the world that was formed. Christ, the origin of all things, is wholly in himself and takes what he is from nowhere else. He is without beginning

and without end. If you consider him through all things, you will find him one in all, and words about him will run out sooner than his nature. What always is has no end at which it ceases in God, and it never began to have a beginning. Yet all this he did for us, coming into the flesh and suffering in the flesh, and God wished us to understand it within ourselves. He is the one author of both testaments, and the divine words must be understood in harmony, fitted to each kind of matter, so that the New Testament agrees with the Old. The two are one, but they are thought to be divided by the very way the law was given, by time and by name: in the Old Testament the offering of cattle and the circumcision of the flesh are required, while in the New only the faith of the mind is sought. So we should recognize in ourselves that in both testaments a perfect man is sought, as it were in two parts, body and spirit, just as Christ was in the flesh. The Old Testament is dedicated to God for the purifying of the body, and the New for the training of the soul.

The two do not disagree with each other. They are divided by reason, so that, just as in these two testaments God is one, so the perfection of good in us may be glory, if the purifying of the body is cultivated by the fruit of the divine will. As the apostle says: “Behold, the old things have passed away and all things have become new.” Elsewhere he says: “As we have borne the image of him who is of clay, so let us bear the image of him who is from heaven.” In the earlier testament, as the present reading teaches, Egypt was struck so that the people of God might be brought into joy, and kinds of cattle, days of the month and a season of the year are required for celebrating the Passover. In the testament called new, the cattle are driven out of the temple in the Gospel, the world is nailed to the cross, and Christ, mounting the gibbet for us, is offered. That one is called the Passover of the Lord; this one is ours. Once we understand how the words are ordered, we may understand that all that is done and has been done for the salvation of men

has been shown for this purpose. The nature of the body is called by the apostle “the form of the world” and “the old man.” It was made by the hand of God, yet because it was taken from clay it is akin to earthly birth. Divided by days and times, years and months and all things under the sun into the natures of the vices, it has dulled the divine race of men with the snares of their earthly dwelling, as the prophet says: “The body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things.” So it must be disciplined by the law of the Old Testament and offered in the tabernacle of God, and then it should owe nothing more to days and times. Like the flesh of Christ, it has become a partner of the virginal body. Before the face of the Lord it must kill the form of sin that works in it. As on the cross of Christ, like a perfect lamb, male and without blemish, it must die, with every vice wholly done away. As the apostle says:

“I have been nailed to the cross with Christ, and now it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” Whoever understands these things is made firm in faith and buried with Christ in baptism through death. Freed from days, times and months, he deserves to be counted among the number of God, not of the world. He despises the earthly things that live, and though he walks in the flesh he does not wage war according to the flesh. He becomes the Passover of the Lord, and reborn in the New Testament he is made like the body of God. When he has offered himself to God as a whole burnt offering, then in what he has suffered he recognizes that Christ, his Passover, has been sacrificed. As Paul says: “If we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also share in his resurrection, knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed and we might no longer be slaves to sin.” And elsewhere he says: “The death he died, he died to sin once for all; but the life he lives, he lives to God.” Finally, our God, taking on flesh, assig[ned] in himself the form of God and of man, that is, of the divine soul and of earthly flesh,

showing that the one is the form of sin and the other is the divine nature. He shows that the one is weapons of wickedness for sin, and the other weapons of righteousness for our salvation. The Word made flesh, though invisible, is seen; though unbegotten, is born; though beyond grasping, is held. He dies as man and rises as God. At one moment he complains, as if afraid, that his soul is sorrowful even unto death; at another, beyond all human confidence, he declares that he will sit at the right hand of God. At one moment he asks that, if possible, the cup of the passion be taken away; at another he insists with confidence that he will drink it, as one received from the Father. At one moment, as man, he complains that God has forsaken him in his sufferings; at another, as God, he promises paradise to the thief who confesses him. He is called a son, and yet Joseph is not his father. He is called a son, and Mary is a virgin before conception, a virgin when she conceives, and, having brought forth the flesh to give the world a miracle, a virgin after the birth.

Among things so different and so discordant, by the understanding of the human creature virginity would not fit with childbearing, death with eternity, distrust with encouragement, or trembling with freedom. He shows one thing to be willing according to the spirit and another to be weak according to the flesh. In this way God willed to be understood as suffering in the flesh for mankind, so that if meaning is sought in us, God is one; if the word, Christ is one; if the work, Jesus is one; if nature is sought, he is the Son; if the beginning is sought, he is called the Father; if creation, he is wisdom; if ministry, an angel; if power, man; if condescension, the Son of Man; if what was made through him, it is life; if what is outside him, nothing. So he ordered all things that, since he was one in all and wished man to be one in himself, whoever searches for him could have no other kind of perfect work than to believe him to be the one God, and to find him almighty in himself, both in what he is and in what he is called. Do not think that it is an insult to the true divinity

if God, commending his love toward us and bearing our weaknesses for us, asks for the offerings of earthly birth. He does not do this to prove that he is in no way distinct from the elements of the world, since the power of eternal infinity goes beyond the grasp of the earthly mind. He does it so that steadfast faith, understanding God through these things, may reject the captious and useless questions of the world and recognize the sin that works in our mortal body. Then man may divide himself, as God shows him everything within him, and discern what must be nailed to the cross with the body disciplined, in order to destroy the work of the world; what in him must be given to God without blemish; and what must be kept beyond suffering, because the divine dwells in us. So, as we said above, being made perfect in God in body, soul and spirit by a threefold work, we may fulfill what is written, as Paul says:

“Just as you presented your members as slaves to impurity for wickedness, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness for sanctification. For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

So look at all these things in yourselves. The working of the things of the world commends their arrangement as beautiful, through the mutual motion of their natures. Yet the Maker must far surpass in glory the understanding of the whole creation, and so you should know that God needed nothing of this kind for himself. But when man was deceived, the demonic nature of idols threw into confusion the simple order of the divine works, which had been distinguished by place, time, number, day, month and reason. It brought in families of uncertain gods and gave the incommunicable name of God to days, months, cattle, birds, wood and stones. Such was this war on faith that men abandoned the God of so great a gift and worshiped the bodily and visible forms of creation in [?]

earthly and heavenly things, as the apostle says of them: “They became futile in their thinking, and their foolish heart was darkened, and they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man and of birds and four-footed beasts and serpents.” So our God had to temper the measure of religious teaching, to make the steep road of divine understanding easier, as if by a gentler slope. First, through the law given by Moses, he forbade every idol in heaven, on earth or in the waters. He condemned the army and principality of the world that works in harmful thoughts, and in these things he disciplined the work of the flesh. With the boundary of the commandment he restrained man, so that he would want nothing as God besides the one God. And when he asked for anything in sacrifice, he did not want the blood of cattle to be shed. He wanted to be killed in us those things that the nature of the vices had taken over with the forms of idols in the flesh, as the apostle says of such things:

“Not that an idol is anything, but what they sacrifice they sacrifice to demons and not to God.” Once these things had been corrected in man, he himself afterward [?] entered the womb of virginal flesh as the place of a perfect man. The forms of idols had been slain in the cattle, and he offered his own blood to redeem and atone for mankind. He passed through all the indignities of our nature, conception, birth, crying and the cradle, and with the world nailed to the cross he might rejoice in man, saved in himself, through himself and for himself. The first month is required for the Passover, but not so that we should pay attention to the month, whose number will clearly perish together with this world that can be numbered. It is required because the Creator of all is in all things, so that what is written may be recognized: “Christ the firstfruits of all.” As for the [?] passage of the enemy: where the first month is required for the sacrifice, there, because, as it is written, “the number of man is the number of the beast,”

the work of the world and [?] in us must first be conquered. Beginning to owe our birth to God rather than to the world, we should understand that our first month and day is not the one on which we appear in the world. It is the one on which Egypt is conquered, that is, the world is renounced, and we are restored to God by a divine birth. We are commanded to observe the course of the moon, but not because religious observance lies in it. Every man is overcome by the things that are seen, and the flesh, akin to the elements and bound to days and times, takes the gods to be rulers of the world. So we must understand that the nature of the elements has been bounded by God in number. Because they wane or wax, we should first believe that they have no power of their own, since they lack freedom to act by their own will. Then, once the teaching of worldly wisdom is rejected, and the law of the decalogue is restored in us in threefold form, in body, soul and spirit, in which man is overcome, the month may become the Lord's, and the birth bounded by time

may be conquered in us. For, as it is written, “the boundaries of the nations were set according to the number of the angels.” When the decade of the world is conquered, the commandments of the Lord's decade are restored. This is why, in the mystery of the Lord, either tithes of the fruits are required in the law, or the tenth day of the month is required to prepare the Passover when Egypt is conquered. He who is mighty in the three recognizes that he has conquered [evice] the beginning, middle and end of the world at work in him, and that he came not to be bound by time but to conquer it. Believing in eternal things, he is made free of time and understands that all the waning and waxing of the sun by day and the moon by night is not the rule of our captivity but the working order of nature. And all that we have lived will be called the Passover of the Lord, not the work of the world, as we return to our own kind. As it is written: “I created all the host of heaven, and I did not command you to worship it.”

An unblemished lamb a year old, taken from the lambs and the kids, is required. This is so that, as it is written, we may imitate the work of Christ, being little children in malice, and act after being steeped in the unblemished law of the Lord. And while man is given back to God, the number of the whole world in a year is conquered, and we may hold fast to the nature of Christ, which cannot be numbered. So, from the lambs and the kids, that is, from two into one new man, once the purifying of body and spirit has been taken up, the Passover of the Lord becomes our Passover too, that is, Christ in man, and man [?] in Christ. Then what is written may be fulfilled: “He who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one.” As for the requirement that the house be purified, it is not the cleansing of a house made by hands that is demanded, since such a house perishes with the age of time. It is as it is written: “We are that house, if we hold firm to the end with the blameless strength of faith.” Nor does God want lintels or doorposts built of wood and stone to be smeared with the blood of a slaughtered beast, for God does not care about such things.

But, as Paul says: “The head of every man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God.” In us he foretells the mystery of the baptism to come, which was to be enriched by the pouring out of divine blood. Some of you already know this, and others of you desire to know it. He wants all that we see, hear, pray or speak, given as if on the doorposts or lintels of the living body, to be made fit for the entrance of the divine word. That is, it should not be carried off into the wandering errors of the world. As we sign ourselves for the glory of the cross of Christ, it should be marked, as with the blood of the unblemished lamb, by the testimony of the divine passion. So, as we walk in newness of life and not in the oldness of the letter, the body we have received in victory will no longer be called the earth of the world but the house of God, not a dwelling of fornication but the image of the body of Christ.
For this reason, you too should understand that the law is spiritual, but we are carnal, sold under sin.

Purify your souls for obedience and offer yourselves as spiritual victims, an acceptable sacrifice pleasing to God. Understand the present reading, and do not gird the loins of the body. As the apostle says, gird the loins of your mind, be sober in all things, and believe perfectly in him in whom you have been sealed by the Spirit. As if cleansing a house, prepare the dwelling of your flesh to be worthy of God's commandments. Imitate the vigils appointed for the Passover of the Lord: while you live in the night of ignorance, keep watch for God, and complete all that you offer before the day of the Lord comes in the morning. If you cannot at once complete what you wish, understand that the neighbor next to you, the one who dwells with you, is the Spirit, and call him to help you finish the work. For, as Paul says, it is he who both wills and works in us and brings it to completion.

The present reading says, in the words of the Lord: “The blood that you have put on the doorposts and lintels will be a sign. When I see this blood I will protect you, and no plague of destruction will fall on you when I strike the land of Egypt.” In the same way, when the Lord comes to judgment, he himself will bear witness for us and cry out in our hearts, “Abba, Father.” Then we will not be condemned with this world, but, sealed on our foreheads with the testimony of the precious blood, we will be acquitted in Christ.

In all these matters the Scriptures of God speak openly to you. Yet because I too am counted your witness in Christ Jesus, I give my counsel as one who has received mercy from the Lord. Let us put off the old man with all his deeds and lusts and become a Passover. In the seven days in which the world is begun, carried on and ended, let us be without leaven, that is, without vice, and sincere, that is, unleavened. Let us owe nothing to the days of the world, keep the nature of God in ourselves and the law, and live by the flesh and blood of the Lord,

so that when God comes to judgment, as you read in the Apocalypse, we may not be the number of the beast or the measure of the world. Instead we may be counted as a book of heavenly teaching, the book over whose seven sealed seals you read that even John wept. Assigned among the twelve thousand sealed in the numbers of the patriarchs, we may be called not the number of the beast but the measure of a man, which is an angel. So what the Lord says in the Gospel will be fulfilled: “The children of this world marry and are given in marriage, beget and are begotten; but the children of God neither marry nor are given in marriage, neither beget nor are begotten, but are like the angels of God.”
TREATISE OF PRISCILLIAN ON THE FIRST PSALM

Holy David established the teaching of divine instruction and laid among men the foundation of the indissoluble word. Rejoicing in everything for which he had been chosen, he set out the work of the first psalm, and in it he both showed the glory of the divine nature and laid down a rule of life for everyone, saying: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence.” Because this psalm is the first and the beginning of all, it necessarily has no title written above it. Whoever has known what was first and has not acted in that way is not held under the title of sin as its possession. As it is written: “For who calls one who is called by himself?” And elsewhere: “The law is not laid down for the righteous.” The prophetic word assigns this to God alone, who alone was able to do it. Yet it also persuades us to serve God, Christ, in such a way that, once the cloud of sins has been wiped away and the birth of Christ has been renewed in us,

we may know that Christ is the beginning of all things and recognize man as the dwelling of Christ, and so prepare a home worthy of such an inhabitant. It should be a home that the error of worldly ambition does not bend, lust does not corrupt and greed does not stain. Enriched with the splendor of everlasting life, it should be found to be the temple of Christ who is God, the covenant of the law and a dwelling worthy of the Savior. As Paul says: “You are the temple of God, and God dwells in you.” And elsewhere: “Know that if anyone violates the temple of God, which you are, God will destroy him.” Understanding this, we know that we are the temple of God and that God dwells in us. So the fear of wrongdoing is greater and the penalty of sin more plain, since the one we have as our daily witness is also our judge, and we owe our death to the one we know to be the author of life. For we are all the body of Christ and individually its members. That we are reborn to salvation is a matter of mercy, not of nature,

so that even if, bound by our birth in the flesh and tied by the vices of the world's evil, we did not escape the way of sinners and the counsels of the ungodly, yet now that we are baptized in Christ and have put on Christ, we may follow the heir of everlasting life. Then we will be found neither sharing with the one we renounced nor unfaithful to the one in whom we believe.

And so, understanding the utterance of the prophetic word, be such as God the Father made you; be such as the Father's hand fashioned you. For the image and likeness of God, which is what you are, does not seek the lures and flatteries of corruption. Nor does it seek any of the counsel of the ungodly and the ways of sinners, the seat of pestilence, the cunning of corrupt flesh and the workshop of a polluted body, as it is written: "The body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that ponders many things." For this is the melody of desire, the blow of anger, an incurable promise, the weapon of the serpent, the craft of the enemy, the flattery of the stranger, the subjugation of ourselves, its own corruption. Through this the enemy who assails us

slips in his arts, and the devil creeps up with snares that deceive by hidden ways, now striking to terrify, now flattering to deceive. So the apostle Paul, showing what he himself wanted and resisting what he did not want to happen, said: "I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and leading me captive in the law of sin." And elsewhere he said: "I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh; for with my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin." So too the prophet, speaking of this, says: "Go up onto a high mountain, you who bring good news to Zion; lift up your voice with strength, you who bring good news to Jerusalem; lift it up, do not fear; say to this people, 'All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is like the flower of grass; the grass has withered and the flower has fallen, but the word of the Lord abides for ever.'" And elsewhere he says: "I will stand upon my watchtower, to see and hear who speaks in me and what I shall answer when I am accused." And elsewhere:

"Hear, my people: those who call you blessed lead you astray and confuse the paths of your feet." If we understand their nature and have no fellowship with their vices, we will necessarily attain the kingdom that flesh and blood will not receive. So Rebecca, chosen for faith in the mystery at work, saw the struggle of two peoples in her womb. In the pain of her labour she brought forth Esau, who was to lose his birthright, and she brought forth Jacob for salvation, the one whom Christ would make heir. In this you too, dearly beloved brothers, as faithful servants and, as it is written, sons of God and fellow heirs with Christ, working to bear witness to what must be spoken, purify your souls for obedience to the faith. Do not conform yourselves to the desires of your life of ignorance, in which you are ashamed [?] to want to receive the wages of sin. Instead, enter on the path of the psalmist's word and walk in the law of the Lord, so that, like the tree planted beside the streams of waters, watered by the springs of the divine

words, you may put forth the branches of a flourishing understanding and the ripe and lasting fruits of an honourable life. These are fruits that the pleasure-seeking season of a corruptible dwelling did not bring forth; they were made fruitful by instruction in the divine word. Then, since the leaves of the commandments do not fall, and we are covered with everlasting light, we may reject the punishments of sinners and have the rest of the righteous, through Jesus Christ.
PRISCILLIAN'S TRACTATE ON THE THIRD PSALM.

"Lord, why have they multiplied who trouble me? Many rise up against me," and the rest. The psalm's title keeps to the order of events: why holy David, holy in spirit [?], turned away from the face of his son Absalom. Yet we who speak of heavenly works must not examine carnal matters. Instead, having tracked down by inquiry what was found in secret, we must obtain the reward for the work we have discovered. As it is written: "Seek," he says, "and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you." And elsewhere: "All things are possible to one who believes." So we must gather by faith the things that were done in outward appearance, and search out visible works in the invisible secret of the mind. For the apostle declares that all things were done in figure and that past events show a type of us. In this way the work of labour, through knowledge of the law, may enlighten those whom ignorance had previously veiled in darkness. As the apostle said to the Ephesians: "For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord; walk as children of light." We must therefore keep watch,

[?] who is joined, who, even if he is corrupted by the passing of time, is yet renewed day by day. So we should count as glorious not what comes before the eyes but what comes into the mind, devoting ourselves not to bodily things but to spiritual ones. We should labour as the apostle Paul teaches, the chosen vessel of Christ and teacher of the Gentiles, who says: "The law," he says, "is spiritual, but I am carnal." And the most blessed Peter says: "Every prophecy or scripture needs interpretation." Hence our meditation night and day in the law of the Lord; hence the eager attention of an inquiring mind upon it, as far as our merit allows. Hence knowledge of ourselves, and hence the confidence to glory in rejecting the things of the flesh and choosing the things of the spirit. Hence we direct the keenness of the heart toward the knowledge of truth, learn the secrets of the heavenly precepts, and provide for the good of the soul while there is still time. So, brothers, as I look more carefully at the providential design of sacred reading, it seems to me that the prophet arranged the order of the psalms with good reason, and that what the Spirit of God dictated was not set out at random.

For first it shows the unformed birth of man, shaped in the simple purity of innocence, equal to the blessed if he remains in that state, when it says: "Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly and has not stood in the way of sinners." Second, it shudders at the poison of envy that has entered the body, when it says: "Why have the nations raged, and the peoples devised vain things?" In the third it teaches that a son's hatred of his father is born from us, showing the things that persecute us. Then there is this too, dearest ones: it has alerted the reader's mind and slowed the anxious mind in its search for the truth by placing at the beginning what he suffered at the end of his reign. I believe it does so to fit the prophecy to the life of man and to mark out the nature of worldly evil. Things tossed by the whirlwinds of ignorance of form or age [?] are bitter with sins; in the calm of later life they ripen through the correction that knowledge brings. For these the same man prays: "The sins of my youth and of my ignorance," he says, "do not remember, O God."

And the apostle, rousing us to the freedom of righteousness and rebuking the slavery of sin in us, says: "For when you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness. What fruit, then, did you have at that time from the things of which you are now ashamed?" This is the third psalm, just as Absalom was the third son. He was ungodly, cruel and unjust: after killing his brother and obtaining pardon, he tried to make war on his devout and most indulgent father, strip him of his kingdom and take his life. I think all of this should be applied to us as a pattern, showing that what we ourselves generate becomes hostile to us. So the first allurement nurtures guilt, and the appearance of evil gives the enemy an opportunity. Then man is driven down the slope of crimes by the impulse of his will, and he is shown to be a man who is a son of perdition. For the first fault is desire, the second is the consent of the will, and the third is carrying out the desired deed. Conversely, in good works we have learned by reading ...
PRISCILLIAN'S TRACTATE TO THE PEOPLE, I.

... to show that he could not do, as the prophet says: "Who is wise, and will perceive these things, and understand and know them? For the ways of the Lord are right, and the righteous will walk in them, but the ungodly will grow weak in them." Therefore you too, clothed in the armour of faith, purify your souls for obedience through the Spirit. Building yourselves up into a temple of the Lord, show simple charity in brotherhood, to the glory of divine love. For it is written: "All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is like the flower of grass; the grass has withered and the flower has fallen, but the word of the Lord abides for ever." And as the Lord says in the gospel: "Enter through the narrow door, for I tell you, many seek to enter and will not be able." This does not mean that the entrance of the saints is made narrow. It means that all friendship with the world is enmity toward God, and human nature is more easily won over by pleasure than by toil. So let us understand that where the desire for present things is pursued, the promise of the future life is not obtained.

So in the gospel the poor woman's coin is more pleasing. Rest is called the bosom of Abraham and of Phinehas [?], while the fire of Gehenna is found to be the dwelling of the merciless rich man. This is not because punishment is laid down absolutely for the rich, or because the wealthy are condemned to despair of returning to the Lord. It is because nothing is achieved all at once at the beginning, and no one has climbed straight up a sheer cliff. As the apostle says: "Charge the rich of this world not to be haughty, nor to hope in uncertain riches, but to be rich in good works." Then, as we make our way toward the Lord through almsgiving and a good life, we may reach the highest things gradually, one step at a time.
PRISCILLIAN'S TRACTATE TO THE PEOPLE, II.

The narrative of the prophetic word is steeped in divine words, and it sets out the deeds named in the title it announces as though they were a proposed theme. It does not speak of the record of mortal times for the instruction of public opinion, since such events always arise from chance movements to which human perception is blind. Rather, in relating the deeds of kingdoms, where one attacks another in order to conquer him, it teaches the one gift that the prophetic work offers us. After we escape the things of the world that belong to the desire of a lost life, we are to keep our conscience free from all fault amid so many wars of vices. We are also to recognize that we owe so great a gift to God our parent. Whoever has recognized that all the prophet endured in persecution, and all that Christ, God, overcame in his passion, was written for our instruction, presses on along the way of the commandments, which is useful and necessary for understanding. Amid so many unexplored troubles of human life and

the measurable battles of the world, which are unworthy of God, let him take up the breastplate of righteousness, the helmet of confidence, the shield of equity and, as it is written, the two-edged sword of the divine mouth. Clothed in the armour of faith and set on fire by the zeal of a burning spirit, let him break the chains of the world and give himself back wholly to the divine nature from which he came, from God Christ, whose debtor he likewise is and to whose image he bears witness. Let him understand that, among the walkways of the divine words, all scripture is the whole man. The gospel word testifies that the entire narrative of events has been fulfilled in us, as Paul also says: "Whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or death or life, all are yours, and you are Christ's, and Christ is God's." For whatever examples we follow while living in the world, whether by training a good character or by the desire of a sinful life, it is with them that we are gathered after death, whether into glory ...

And so whoever has turned to the faith of Christ and come to know the first, middle and last things, all that was done through the Lord and all that is still to come, must separate the temporary from the everlasting, the false from the true, and the passing from the certain. When he sees that he is of divine race, he holds to the one God, who is the same to him in every way [?], and rejoices in the things that are subject neither to beginning nor to end. Holy David, trusting in God, acted amid the uncertainties of battle and the slaughter of wars with foreigners. Such a man does not take all this as a memorial written about the world. He recognizes what power there is in us, partly from our own fear and partly from the body's fear, in the wars of daily sins and the variety of worldly desires, while we pursue uncertain things instead of certain ones and strive among things alien to us. As David himself says in the psalms: "Lord, free me from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others, for I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is ever before me." For all things

that were done or written were written so that the mind of God, showing invisible things through visible ones, might speak in language best suited to human understanding. Then every man who sought God might see in the scriptures what was acceptable to God: in the choosing of a people, a homeland and prophets, and in place, time, day, month, delight and struggle. If he ordered his life by the things God had provided and advanced to the standing of devout understanding, he would recognize that everything written was written about himself. Walking in newness of life, whether something was granted to powers or to kings, he would grasp this one thing from the voices of the prophets: whatever is friendly to the world is found to be hostile to Christ. As the apostle says: "All friendship with the world is enmity toward God." And again: "All the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes and the ambition of human life are not from the Father but from this world, and the world is passing away, and its desire too,

but the word of the Lord abides for ever." The weakness of human understanding compels us to seek, in the utterances of prophetic speech, the outward forms of earthly things as signs of higher powers. In this way, prompted by our familiarity with visible things, we may widen the narrow limits of human weakness toward meanings we are not used to, devoutly hoping to learn. Yet nature itself teaches us that these are the things which, after we have turned to faith, either fight against us or rule within us, through the distress of fear or the flattery of good fortune. So we build up again what we had torn down and return to what we had renounced. For it makes no difference to the devil whether fear of evils or the lure of good fortune supplies the occasion and material of sin for a life estranged from God. The only difference is that, in our captivity, growing used to misery is now easier to bear than the ruin of the prosperous,
as the prophet says about this: "Hear me, my people: as your taskmasters cheat you, so those who call you blessed lead you astray, to confuse the paths of your feet."

And so holy David introduces the title of the psalm, set down for the instruction of those who have turned to God, in the exultation of a man triumphing after the defeat of the two Syrias. The reader is to recognize that the title set down for instruction, and David's thanksgiving at being saved in the midst of wars, point to the meaning of the prophetic word. Taking up the work of divine understanding and seeing in himself the wars of his own desires, he should then reject the errors of human weakness. He should conquer the two Syrias, that is, the two sources of sin, since the will or the act of doing something worldly comes through the working of one, the soul, or of the other, the body. Clothed, as it is written, in the armour of faith, he should celebrate a triumph over the vices. As if receiving the pay of a victorious campaign, he should earn the unfading crown of a life dedicated in Christ,

since this is the glory of perfect good: if, as it is written, the chastening of the body is cultivated at the price of the will. And so, as long as there is no end among us to things without limit, and, with our step set on slippery ground, we fix no measure for uncertain things, we are taught even by the words of the apostle that the wars of daily struggles are waged within us. Paul says to us: The flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; these contend with one another, so that we do not do what we wish. And because the sense of human understanding and the reasoning of common opinion could not at once take in the apostle's word and the heavenly counsel, the apostle Paul goes on to show why, when we sin, the flesh, conquered by vices, and the ambition of human life are made subject, saying: Your struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities and powers of this world, the rulers of this darkness,

against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. So too John says: I saw three unclean spirits like three frogs coming out of the mouth of the false prophet and out of the mouth of the beast; and these are three spirits of demons, which go out to throw the kings of the earth into confusion. And again David himself, showing what was fighting within us, says: Lord, I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is ever against me. And the apostle, speaking of this, says: Where do wars come from, where do quarrels among you come from? Do they not come from your desires, which wage war in your members? The aim was that whoever wished to have the work of the divine commandments in him should conquer all the wars of the vices within himself and abstain from the lusts not only of the flesh but also of the thoughts, that is, of spiritual wickedness; and that, despising the sorceries of the pagan demons within him, he should recognize to whom man, given over to the world, owed the tributes of sins, to whom the wages of vices, to whom the fears of terrors, to whom the honours of passing dignities,

and that, rejecting all the things whose end is death and in which he is rebuked and taught, and owing his whole self to God, he should himself become what the psalm is and enter into the exultation of the psalmist's words, as David says: O God, you have cast us off and destroyed us; you were angry, and you had mercy on us. In these words of the psalm, however, the mind turned to God is carried beyond the reach of natural understanding, and to each one who understands, the [?] of incorruptible blessedness is opened through them. For at this point, in such words of the psalm, it is good to cry out against the cunning of the devil who lies in wait, with the free voice of man saved in Christ: Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O death, is your victory? See, when God rebukes, he loves, and he instructs through the recognition of sin rather than punishing. And since you, death, have no other nature than either to drive us into the evils of sin or, once your victim has been struck and caught by the poison, to press him hard into the things you yourself have urged on him, we learn, as Christ teaches, that we who are baptized in Christ,

when we are destroyed in what is alien to God, are remade in what is properly our own; and that what is punishment for those who go on sinning to the end is, for us who have turned back, teaching through rebuke. As David himself says: Who is like you, O Lord? For you have shown me tribulations, and, turning, you gave me life and taught me. And again Isaiah says: Lord, we conceived in the womb and brought forth the spirit of salvation which you have given upon the earth. Here we ourselves prove within ourselves what kind of man he ought to be who, living by faith in a new birth, governs his mind toward things worthy of God's substance. Yet the ordering of the Scriptures used the examples of deeds as incorruptible testimonies for our understanding, so that, in commending the love of God in us, it might more easily show the opinions about mortal things that fight together within us, if it proved what it said through forms of words and parables of things.

Thus Rebecca, mother of a blessed womb and bearing the decrees of the divine promise, showed the works of the world and of God struggling with each other within us. When she could not bear the fighting within her womb, she burst out in a prophecy of free sorrow, saying: Why is this happening to me, if it is so? The voice of the Lord answered her and taught her: Two peoples and two nations are in your womb. The apostle Paul too makes this plain when he explains it, saying: I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and leading me captive into the law of sin. And in order to show, in the two nations and two peoples, what the people and nation of God was and what the people of the vices was, he wished the old man to be stripped from us with all his deeds and lusts, and us to be remade into the new, saying: As we have borne the image of him who is of clay, let us bear the image of him who is from heaven. Thus whoever believed himself to be of divine race would despise earthly things, follow Christ, and consecrate himself to heavenly glories.

So the two testaments set forth for faith, the one loosing the yoke of slavery, the other dispensing the work of grace, bore the names old and new. The one man placed within both, possessing in himself the work both of the divine nature and of earthly flesh (since there is no fellowship of light with darkness, of Christ with Belial), was meant to restrain by the law of discipline what belonged to the flesh, and not to deny himself to God, whose image and likeness had appeared. So, understand, on one side the discipline of the curse was set up, on the other the grace of blessings. Although there are many dwelling places with our God, and he wills all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, none of you should be unaware that the conduct of our life lies between two kingdoms, between the synagogue of Satan and the church of God's commandments, that is, between the works of the world and the words of God. What belongs to God is called ours,

while what belongs to the world, being contrary to God, is for that reason found to be alien to us as well; that we renounce, this we believe. And so, as we stand among such things, on this side presses the promise of the divine commandments, on that the purpose of the devil's temptation; on this side the faith of Christ urges us, on that the faithlessness of the world; on this side peace, patience, long-suffering, gentleness and the rest of that kind; on that side anger, the sister of avarice; fornication, the friend of darkness; ambition, blind to its own fortune; the guarding of riches, made more wretched by greed; fury, which knows nothing of God; the pleasure of belly and throat; glorying in shameful things; the desire of the eyes; and the seemingly innocent persuasion of the devil's pomp in the deceit of the shows. While man is dragged this way and that into these things, the choice of life and death being set before us, we know nothing of the battles and wars of the world within us for as long as, living in God and refuting what is alien, we hold fast to the Lord's words.

For if we acknowledge that we are being rebuked and overcome what is against us, we must walk in newness; and, as the text of the psalm shows, having received the wine of compunction, we escape the bow and the arrows of the devil who pursues us, recognizing that we cannot be free from sins unless we are saved by the remission of baptism and the redemption of the divine cross. In this part of the psalmist's words, those whom steadfast faith calls to the pursuit of truth should not merely take it in by hearing but look into it with understanding. They should see how the psalm adapts itself to every weakness of our understanding, and, tempering the manner of its prophetic work through the arrangement of its words, softens the steep road of divine understanding as though into a gentler slope and makes the climb easier. For those converted to the faith find it easier to know the evils of their own sins than to understand the dispensation of the divine nature within them, and it comes more readily to man not to will sin than to will what is divine.

So in the psalm an order best suited to the progress of its readers follows. The knowledge of himself is kept back for God until later in the psalm, since he is not known except through himself. First, the Lord's rebuke, that is, the recognition of sin, opens the way for the divine gift; and when man, become a dwelling for his own nature, recognizes what God wills, the word of the meaningful history follows, saying: God has spoken in his holy place. Thus whoever had sanctified himself to God, with the Lord speaking in him, would hear God speaking in his holy place [?]; and, measuring by the laws of his own nature everything that human virtue was thought to have done in the histories of the saints, he would weigh it among the divine declarations of the testimony given about himself. So the prophetic word, speaking once yet proclaiming two things, carries about as a twin emblem the exultation of man saved in Christ and the glory of Christ triumphing in man, and opens them for the teaching that instructs us, so that, as we learn the deeds of the saints,

we may hold fast the triumph of a good life, now that the ordering of what was said has been fully set out. For Shechem, whose dividing is the joy of man and of Christ, is a land of foreign regions. There the daughter of Jacob, the chosen man, was seized on the occasion of a passing journey; captivated by what her eyes saw, she gazed in wonder at foreign things and lost both the dignity of the chosen race and the glory of virginity. Shechem, punished in vengeance for the crime committed, is divided, and, as a memorial and a testimony, lest God's people do any such thing among foreigners [?], it is made subject. Ephraim and Manasseh are the two sons of holy Joseph, whom he earned, once Egypt had been made subject to him, for the fruitfulness of offspring, as for the fruit of perfect truth. Gilead held their firstfruits. From Judah, from whom a king is sought, God was born in the flesh. And because Ruth the Moabitess, by persevering in faith, earned a divine lineage in her conceiving, Moab is called the tabernacle of hope.

Edom is the land of faithlessness, where the shoe of the divine journey is stretched out. The Philistines, when the idol Dagon was overthrown at the release of the ark of the Lord, are made subject to the divine array. Through all these things the reasoning of our teaching reaches out and shows the work of God saving in Christ and the path of sanctified man. For Shechem is conquered and the valleys of the tabernacles are measured out if, as we believe in Christ born of a virgin, the nature of carnal lust, which was the cause of corruption, is also conquered, and if the body, given back not to fornication but to the Lord and divided by the immortal words of the commandments, is counted worthy of Christ's tabernacles and the glories of the future resurrection. And so, once the world has been conquered as Egypt was made subject, fruit is given to those who labour in Ephraim and Manasseh, and no leader is sought except from Judah. For those saved by the passion of Christ, nothing else
